subjects.name: Anatomy & Embryology
lectureNames: Blood Vessels and Nerves of the Pelvis
Congenital Anomalies of the Genital System

questions.text: How can you orient an isolated kidney to identify whether it is right or left?
questions.explanation: Use the inferior ureter to establish the vertical axis, then use the medial hilum and posterior renal pelvis to distinguish the sides.
questions.modelAnswer: The hilum faces medially, the renal pelvis lies posterior to the renal vessels, and the ureter descends inferiorly.

questions.text: List the posterior relations of the kidneys. Include the muscles, ribs, and nearby nerves and vessels, and distinguish right from left where appropriate.
questions.explanation: The left kidney sits higher, so its posterior relations include both the 11th and 12th ribs.
questions.modelAnswer: The diaphragm lies superiorly. The right kidney relates to the 12th rib and the left to the 11th and 12th ribs. Below the diaphragm are psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transversus abdominis. The subcostal vessels and nerve and the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves cross the posterior region.

questions.text: List the main visceral relations of the anterior surface of the right kidney.
questions.explanation: The descending duodenum lies near the medial border; the liver covers a large anterior area lateral to it.
questions.modelAnswer: The right suprarenal gland, descending (second) part of the duodenum, right lobe of the liver, right colic flexure, and loops of small intestine.

questions.text: List the main visceral relations of the anterior surface of the left kidney.
questions.explanation: The pancreas crosses the anterior surface near its middle. The stomach and spleen relate to the upper part, and the colon and jejunum lie lower down.
questions.modelAnswer: The left suprarenal gland, spleen, stomach, body of pancreas with splenic vessels, left colic flexure and adjacent descending colon, and coils of jejunum.

questions.text: List the four coverings of the kidney in order from the kidney outward.
questions.explanation: Perirenal fat lies inside the renal fascia and surrounds the kidney. Pararenal fat lies outside the fascia.
questions.modelAnswer: Fibrous renal capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, then pararenal fat.

questions.text: Name the parent vessel of each renal artery and the receiving vessel of each renal vein.
questions.explanation: The principal renal vessels connect the kidneys to the abdominal aorta and inferior vena cava. The right renal artery runs behind the vena cava.
questions.modelAnswer: Each renal artery arises from the abdominal aorta. Each renal vein drains to the inferior vena cava.

questions.text: Where does renal lymph drain, and what plexus carries the kidney's vasomotor innervation?
questions.explanation: The lymphatics follow the renal vessels toward the aorta. The renal plexus accompanies the renal artery.
questions.modelAnswer: Renal lymph drains to the lateral aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes. The renal plexus carries the vasomotor sympathetic fibers.

questions.text: Name the principal structures posterior to the abdominal ureter and the vessel behind it as it crosses the pelvic brim.
questions.explanation: The ureter descends on the psoas region before crossing the iliac vessels to enter the pelvis.
questions.modelAnswer: The abdominal ureter lies anterior to psoas major and the genitofemoral nerve. Psoas minor may also be present. At the pelvic brim it passes in front of the distal common iliac artery or the origin of the external iliac artery.

questions.text: List the main anterior relations of the abdominal part of the right ureter.
questions.explanation: The retroperitoneal ureter lies behind the right mesenteric root; several named vessels cross it anteriorly.
questions.modelAnswer: The third part of the duodenum, right gonadal vessels, right colic and ileocolic vessels, root of the small-intestinal mesentery with superior mesenteric vessels, and terminal ileum.

questions.text: List the main anterior relations of the abdominal part of the left ureter.
questions.explanation: The left ureter lies retroperitoneally. Left colic and sigmoid branches and the sigmoid mesocolon cross it anteriorly.
questions.modelAnswer: The left gonadal vessels, left colic and sigmoid vessels, and sigmoid colon with its mesocolon.

questions.text: Name the structures that the pelvic ureter crosses along the lateral pelvic wall before turning medially toward the bladder.
questions.explanation: The ureter descends along the lateral pelvic wall toward the level of the ischial spine before turning medially.
questions.modelAnswer: It crosses the fascia covering obturator internus, external iliac vessels, obliterated umbilical artery, and the obturator nerve and vessels.

questions.text: Name the principal arteries supplying the abdominal and pelvic portions of the ureter. Distinguish the male and female pelvic contributions.
questions.explanation: The ureter receives blood segmentally from nearby vessels. The named pelvic branches differ with the surrounding reproductive anatomy.
questions.modelAnswer: The abdominal ureter receives branches from the renal, gonadal, and common iliac arteries and the abdominal aorta. The inferior vesical artery supplies the pelvic ureter in males. Uterine and vaginal arteries contribute in females.

questions.text: Name the three traditionally described sites of ureteric narrowing.
questions.explanation: These sites correspond to the transition from renal pelvis to ureter, the pelvic brim crossing, and the passage through the bladder wall.
questions.modelAnswer: The ureteropelvic junction, the pelvic brim at the crossing of the iliac vessels, and the intramural ureter at the ureterovesical junction.

questions.text: What does the median umbilical ligament connect, and what embryonic structure forms it?
questions.explanation: The unpaired median umbilical ligament is the urachal remnant. The paired medial umbilical ligaments are remnants of the umbilical arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: It connects the apex of the urinary bladder to the umbilicus and is the fibrous remnant of the urachus.

questions.text: Describe the relations of the bladder fundus in males, including the structures between the fundus and rectum.
questions.explanation: The rectovesical pouch is the upper peritoneal reflection; below it the genital ducts and seminal vesicles separate the bladder from the rectum.
questions.modelAnswer: The rectum lies posteriorly. The seminal vesicles and ampullae of the ductus deferens intervene, and the rectovesical pouch relates to the upper part.

questions.text: In females, what structure lies immediately posterior to the base of the urinary bladder?
questions.explanation: The base is the posterior aspect of the bladder. In females it lies against the anterior vaginal wall.
questions.modelAnswer: The anterior wall of the vagina.

questions.text: What structures relate to the inferolateral surfaces of the urinary bladder, and what separates them from it?
questions.explanation: The inferolateral bladder surfaces are extraperitoneal and lie against the retropubic tissue and pelvic wall.
questions.modelAnswer: The pubic bones, obturator internus and levator ani relate to these surfaces. Retropubic fat intervenes anteriorly and laterally.

questions.text: Name the true ligaments of the urinary bladder in the course classification. Give the corresponding male and female terms.
questions.explanation: These are fibrous or fascial supports. The similarly named umbilical peritoneal folds are classified separately in the course.
questions.modelAnswer: The median umbilical ligament, the medial and lateral puboprostatic ligaments in males, and the corresponding pubovesical ligaments in females.

questions.text: List the principal arteries to the urinary bladder in males and females and name three additional arterial contributors.
questions.explanation: The superior vesical contribution is shared. The inferior contribution differs with the surrounding pelvic structures.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior vesical arteries supply the bladder in both sexes. Inferior vesical arteries contribute in males and vaginal arteries in females. Additional branches come from the obturator, inferior gluteal and middle rectal arteries.

questions.text: Which lymph nodes receive most lymph from the urinary bladder, and what are the other pelvic drainage groups listed in the course?
questions.explanation: The external iliac group receives most bladder lymph. Other pelvic routes account for the remaining drainage.
questions.modelAnswer: Most drains to the external iliac nodes. Additional drainage reaches the internal iliac, obturator and common iliac nodes.

questions.text: What are the sympathetic and parasympathetic spinal sources of urinary bladder innervation?
questions.explanation: These autonomic pathways reach the bladder through the pelvic plexus. Voluntary sphincter control is a separate somatic pathway.
questions.modelAnswer: Sympathetic fibers arise from the lower thoracic and upper lumbar segments. Parasympathetic fibers arise from S2–S4 and travel in the pelvic splanchnic nerves.

questions.text: Which nerve provides somatic motor supply to the external urethral sphincter, and what are its sacral roots?
questions.explanation: The external urethral sphincter contains skeletal muscle and is under somatic control. The pelvic splanchnic nerves carry parasympathetic fibers to pelvic viscera.
questions.modelAnswer: The pudendal nerve, from S2–S4.

questions.text: Name the widest and narrowest segments of the male urethra and its narrowest opening.
questions.explanation: The external meatus is a single opening. The membranous part is an entire urethral segment.
questions.modelAnswer: The prostatic urethra is the widest segment. The membranous urethra is the narrowest segment. The external urethral meatus is the narrowest opening.

questions.text: Compare the approximate adult lengths of the male and female urethra.
questions.explanation: The male urethra extends through the prostate, perineum and penis. The female urethra follows a much shorter course from the bladder to the vestibule.
questions.modelAnswer: The male urethra is about 18–20 cm, and the female urethra is about 4 cm.

questions.text: In which body regions do the pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros first develop in the course model?
questions.explanation: The three nephric systems appear in a cranial-to-caudal sequence along intermediate mesoderm.
questions.modelAnswer: The pronephros develops in the cervical region, the mesonephros in the thoracic and upper lumbar regions, and the metanephros in the lower lumbar and sacral regions.

questions.text: Name the two main female remnants of mesonephric tubules described in the course.
questions.explanation: These are remnants of mesonephric tubules. Gartner duct derives from the mesonephric duct.
questions.modelAnswer: The epoophoron and paroophoron.

questions.text: How can failure of ureteric bud development cause renal agenesis?
questions.explanation: The ureteric bud and metanephric mesenchyme depend on developmental signaling between them. Loss of that interaction can prevent normal kidney formation.
questions.modelAnswer: If the ureteric bud does not develop or fails to reach the metanephric mesenchyme, it cannot induce nephron development. The kidney fails to form.

questions.text: Where do the levator prostatae fibers of levator ani insert?
questions.explanation: The anterior medial fibers of pubococcygeus pass around the prostate to reach the perineal body.
questions.modelAnswer: The perineal body.

questions.text: List the three principal branches of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery.
questions.explanation: These branches supply the posterolateral pelvic wall, sacral region and superior gluteal region.
questions.modelAnswer: Iliolumbar artery, lateral sacral arteries and superior gluteal artery.

questions.text: Which artery continues into the pelvis as the superior rectal artery?
questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery is the terminal continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery and supplies the upper rectal region.
questions.modelAnswer: The inferior mesenteric artery.

questions.text: From which surface of the abdominal aorta, and at what relation to its bifurcation, does the median sacral artery usually arise?
questions.explanation: The vessel descends in the midline along the anterior surface of the sacrum.
questions.modelAnswer: It arises from the posterior surface of the abdominal aorta just above the aortic bifurcation.

questions.text: Near the uterine tube, with which artery do terminal uterine artery branches anastomose?
questions.explanation: Tubal and ovarian branches of the uterine artery communicate with branches of the ovarian artery in the upper broad ligament.
questions.modelAnswer: The ovarian artery.

questions.text: Where do the right and left ovarian or testicular veins normally drain?
questions.explanation: This left–right asymmetry applies to both ovarian and testicular venous drainage.
questions.modelAnswer: The right ovarian or testicular vein drains into the inferior vena cava. The left drains into the left renal vein.

questions.text: Which lumbar spinal levels contribute to the obturator nerve?
questions.explanation: The obturator nerve arises from the anterior divisions of the ventral rami of L2–L4 in the lumbar plexus.
questions.modelAnswer: L2, L3 and L4.

questions.text: Name the two triangles of the perineum and the line that divides them.
questions.explanation: The interischial line crosses the widest part of the diamond-shaped perineal region.
questions.modelAnswer: A line joining the ischial tuberosities separates the anterior urogenital triangle and the posterior anal triangle.

questions.text: What type of nerve fibers innervate the dartos muscle, and through which named branch do they reach it?
questions.explanation: Dartos is smooth muscle in the scrotal wall. Its contraction wrinkles the scrotal skin.
questions.modelAnswer: Sympathetic fibers reach the dartos through the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve.

questions.text: From which layers of the abdominal wall do the external and internal spermatic fasciae derive?
questions.explanation: The coverings reflect the layers encountered at the superficial and deep inguinal rings during testicular descent.
questions.modelAnswer: The external spermatic fascia derives from the external oblique aponeurosis. The internal spermatic fascia derives from transversalis fascia.

questions.text: Which embryonic peritoneal outpouching forms the tunica vaginalis, and what normally happens to its proximal segment?
questions.explanation: Obliteration closes the communication between the peritoneal cavity and the distal sac around the testis.
questions.modelAnswer: The distal processus vaginalis persists as the tunica vaginalis. Its proximal segment normally obliterates.

questions.text: Name the three coverings of the spermatic cord in order from superficial to deep.
questions.explanation: The deepest of these coverings is derived from transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring.
questions.modelAnswer: External spermatic fascia, cremasteric muscle and fascia, then internal spermatic fascia.

questions.text: Compare the principal lymphatic drainage of penile skin and the glans penis in the course description.
questions.explanation: The course separates cutaneous drainage from the deeper route that carries lymph from the glans.
questions.modelAnswer: Penile skin drains to superficial inguinal nodes. The glans drains to deep inguinal and external iliac nodes.

questions.text: Which vessels does the ductus deferens hook around after it passes through the deep inguinal ring into the pelvis?
questions.explanation: The ductus deferens turns medially after entering the pelvis at the deep inguinal ring.
questions.modelAnswer: The inferior epigastric vessels.

questions.text: Where does the urethra enter the prostate, and where does it emerge from the gland?
questions.explanation: The course describes an entry at the base and an exit on the anterior surface just above the apex.
questions.modelAnswer: It enters through the base near its anterior border. It emerges from the anterior surface anterosuperior to the apex.

questions.text: Describe a venous route by which prostate carcinoma can spread to vertebral bodies.
questions.explanation: Communication between the pelvic and vertebral venous plexuses provides a route to the spine.
questions.modelAnswer: The prostatic venous plexus communicates with the internal vertebral venous plexus through the lateral sacral veins.

questions.text: Which external male genital structure is homologous to the labia majora?
questions.explanation: Both structures develop from the labioscrotal swellings.
questions.modelAnswer: The scrotum.

questions.text: What is the name of the median cleft between the two labia majora?
questions.explanation: The cleft is between the labia majora. The vestibule lies between the labia minora.
questions.modelAnswer: The pudendal cleft.

questions.text: Name the principal openings found in the vulvar vestibule in the course anatomy description.
questions.explanation: The vestibule is between the labia minora. The greater vestibular glands communicate with it through their ducts.
questions.modelAnswer: The external urethral meatus, the vaginal opening, and the openings of the greater vestibular gland ducts.

questions.text: Which lymph node group receives most superficial lymphatic drainage from the vulva?
questions.explanation: The superficial vulvar lymphatics drain chiefly toward the groin.
questions.modelAnswer: The superficial inguinal lymph nodes.

questions.text: Where do the lateral and medial regions of the breast mainly drain lymph in the course model?
questions.explanation: The lateral route involves the axilla. Medial lymphatics follow vessels toward the internal thoracic chain.
questions.modelAnswer: The lateral region drains mainly to the anterior or pectoral axillary nodes. The medial region drains mainly to parasternal or internal thoracic nodes.

questions.text: Which two arteries contribute to the arterial supply of the ovary?
questions.explanation: The ovarian branch of the uterine artery anastomoses with branches of the ovarian artery near the ovary.
questions.modelAnswer: The ovarian artery from the abdominal aorta and the ovarian branch of the uterine artery.

questions.text: To which lymph nodes does the ovary primarily drain according to the course text?
questions.explanation: Ovarian lymphatics travel with the ovarian vessels toward the aorta.
questions.modelAnswer: The lateral aortic and preaortic lumbar nodes.

questions.text: Which part of the uterine tube passes through the uterine wall, and how does its length and caliber compare with the other parts?
questions.explanation: This short segment traverses the uterine wall and opens into the uterine cavity.
questions.modelAnswer: The intramural or interstitial part. It is the shortest and narrowest part.

questions.text: What does anteflexion of the uterus describe?
questions.explanation: Anteflexion concerns the angle between the uterine body and cervix. Anteversion concerns the orientation of the uterus relative to the vagina.
questions.modelAnswer: The uterine body bends forward relative to the cervix at the internal os.

questions.text: Which vaginal fornix is covered by peritoneum from the rectouterine pouch?
questions.explanation: Peritoneum descends behind the cervix to the posterior vaginal fornix, which is related to the rectouterine pouch.
questions.modelAnswer: The posterior vaginal fornix.

questions.text: How does the cavity of the uterine body appear in coronal and sagittal sections?
questions.explanation: In coronal section the tubal openings mark the two upper corners and the internal os lies at the inferior apex.
questions.modelAnswer: It is triangular in coronal section and slit-like in sagittal section.

questions.text: Name the four parts of the broad ligament in the designated anatomy text.
questions.explanation: The mesovarium attaches to the ovary, the mesosalpinx supports the uterine tube, and the mesometrium is the larger uterine portion. The infundibulopelvic part reaches the lateral pelvic wall.
questions.modelAnswer: Mesovarium, mesosalpinx, mesometrium, and the infundibulopelvic part (suspensory ligament of the ovary).

questions.text: Which artery does the round ligament of the uterus hook around before entering the deep inguinal ring in its course toward the labium majus?
questions.explanation: The round ligament runs anterolaterally to the deep ring and then traverses the inguinal canal.
questions.modelAnswer: The inferior epigastric artery.

questions.text: Name the five groups of branches of the uterine artery described in the course anatomy text.
questions.explanation: The artery first gives cervical and vaginal branches, ascends along the uterus, and then runs laterally toward the tube and ovary.
questions.modelAnswer: Cervical, vaginal, uterine, tubal, and ovarian branches.

questions.text: Which vaginal wall is longer?
questions.explanation: The cervix projects into the upper anterior wall of the vagina. The posterior fornix extends farther superiorly.
questions.modelAnswer: The posterior vaginal wall.

questions.text: How do primordial germ cells reach the genital ridges from the region of the hindgut?
questions.explanation: The dorsal mesentery is part of the migration route to the developing gonads.
questions.modelAnswer: They migrate by amoeboid movement along the dorsal mesentery of the hindgut.

questions.text: Which fetal testicular cells produce anti-Müllerian hormone, and what does it do to the paramesonephric ducts?
questions.explanation: Anti-Müllerian hormone acts on the paramesonephric duct system. The mesonephric duct develops under a separate androgen-dependent pathway.
questions.modelAnswer: Fetal Sertoli cells produce anti-Müllerian hormone, which induces regression of the paramesonephric ducts.

questions.text: In the course embryology chapter, which failed connection is used to explain cystic dilatation of seminiferous tubules in polycystic testis?
questions.explanation: The efferent ductules normally provide outflow from the rete testis. Failure of that connection can lead to cystic dilatation in the developmental model described.
questions.modelAnswer: Failure of the rete testis to connect with the efferent ductules.

questions.text: What name is given to a persistent processus vaginalis in females?
questions.explanation: The female processus vaginalis usually obliterates. The name canal of Nuck refers to persistence of that peritoneal extension.
questions.modelAnswer: The canal of Nuck.

questions.text: What do the genital tubercle, urethral folds, and genital swellings form during development of the female external genitalia?
questions.explanation: These are three distinct primordia. The urethral folds remain unfused in the usual female developmental pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: The genital tubercle becomes the clitoris, the urethral folds become the labia minora, and the genital swellings become the labia majora.

questions.text: Name the accessory gland derived from the caudal buds of the urogenital sinus in each sex.
questions.explanation: The caudal buds form the bulbourethral glands in males and the homologous greater vestibular glands in females.
questions.modelAnswer: Male: bulbourethral glands (Cowper glands). Female: greater vestibular glands (Bartholin glands).

questions.text: Compare the lymphatic drainage of the female urethra with that of the prostatic, membranous and spongy parts of the male urethra.
questions.explanation: The drainage of the male urethra differs by segment. The spongy part has predominantly inguinal drainage, while the two named proximal segments and the female urethra have internal iliac drainage in the course description.
questions.modelAnswer: The female urethra and the male prostatic and membranous urethra drain to the internal iliac lymph nodes. The male spongy urethra drains predominantly to the deep inguinal lymph nodes, with a minority of vessels reaching the superficial inguinal nodes.

questions.text: Which vessel crosses anterior to the abdominal ureter on the same side?
questions.explanation: The ovarian vessels pass anterior to the abdominal ureter. At the pelvic brim, the ureter itself passes anterior to the iliac vessels.

questions.text: In the conventional three-site description, where is the first ureteric narrowing encountered from the kidney?
questions.explanation: The first site is where the renal pelvis narrows into the ureter. The iliac crossing and intramural segment occur farther downstream.
options: Intramural ureter in the bladder wall

questions.text: Which landmark identifies the middle ureteric narrowing in the conventional three-site description?
questions.explanation: The traditional middle narrowing is at the iliac vessel crossing as the ureter enters the pelvis. The ischial spine is a separate landmark farther down in the pelvis.
options: The point where the renal pelvis ends
The place where the ureter enters the bladder wall
The level of the ischial spine
The iliac vessel crossing at the pelvic brim

questions.text: Where is the most distal of the three conventionally described ureteric narrowings?
questions.explanation: The distal site is the intramural segment, where the ureter passes obliquely through the bladder wall before opening into its lumen.
options: At the junction with the renal pelvis
At the level of the ischial spine

questions.text: Which muscle lies immediately posterior to the abdominal ureter along most of its descent?
questions.explanation: The abdominal ureter descends on the anterior surface of psoas major. The genitofemoral nerve also descends on that muscle.

questions.text: Which lymph node group receives most of the lymphatic drainage from the male spongy urethra in the course description?
questions.explanation: The spongy urethra drains predominantly to the deep inguinal nodes. A minority of its lymphatic vessels pass to superficial inguinal nodes. The prostatic and membranous urethra drain to internal iliac nodes.

questions.text: Which duct forms when the ductus deferens joins the duct of the seminal vesicle?
questions.explanation: The ejaculatory duct forms at the union of the ductus deferens and the seminal vesicle duct, then traverses the prostate to open into the prostatic urethra.

questions.text: When the uterine artery crosses the ureter near the cervix, where is the ureter relative to the artery?
questions.explanation: The uterine artery crosses above the ureter near the cervix. The ureter is therefore at risk during ligation of the uterine artery.
options: At the same level, anterior to the artery
At the same level, posterior to the artery

questions.text: What is the apex of a renal pyramid called?
questions.explanation: The renal papilla is the tip of a medullary pyramid. Papillary ducts open there and discharge urine into a minor calyx.

questions.text: Which ducts open into the prostatic sinuses on either side of the urethral crest?
questions.explanation: The prostatic ducts open into the prostatic sinuses. The ejaculatory ducts open near the prostatic utricle on the seminal colliculus.

questions.text: Which space lies between the pubic symphysis and the urinary bladder?
questions.explanation: The retropubic space contains extraperitoneal fat anterior to the bladder. The vesicouterine pouch is a peritoneal reflection between the bladder and uterus.

questions.text: Which embryonic structure gives rise to the urachus?
questions.explanation: The intraembryonic allantois narrows between the bladder apex and umbilicus to form the urachus. Its fibrous remnant is the median umbilical ligament.

questions.text: A 3-year-old girl has persistent leakage of urine from the umbilicus.
questions.explanation: A persistent connection between the bladder apex and the umbilicus explains the urinary leakage. The case also tests the normal embryologic origins of the bladder and female urethral epithelium.
questions.modelAnswer: A persistent connection between the bladder apex and the umbilicus explains the urinary leakage. The case also tests the normal embryologic origins of the bladder and female urethral epithelium.

subQuestions.text: What anomaly explains the umbilical leakage?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Patent urachus, also called an urachal fistula.
subQuestions.explanation: A patent urachus leaves a continuous channel from the bladder apex to the umbilicus.

subQuestions.text: Describe the embryologic origins of the urinary bladder wall, including the traditional account of the trigone.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The vesical part of the primitive urogenital sinus supplies most bladder epithelium. In the traditional account, incorporation of the caudal mesonephric ducts contributes to the trigone, and urogenital sinus endoderm later covers it. Surrounding splanchnic mesoderm forms the rest of the wall.
subQuestions.explanation: Separate epithelial origin, the contribution of the distal mesonephric ducts in the traditional model, and the mesodermal origin of muscle and connective tissue.

subQuestions.text: What is the embryologic origin of the female urethral epithelium in the course description?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Endoderm of the vesical part of the primitive urogenital sinus.
subQuestions.explanation: The course attributes female urethral epithelium to the primitive urogenital sinus.

questions.text: Which surface of the male bladder is partly covered by peritoneum continuous with the rectovesical pouch?
questions.explanation: The upper base of the male bladder has a peritoneal covering associated with the rectovesical pouch. The inferolateral surfaces and neck have no peritoneal covering.
options: The inferior part of its neck
The upper part of its base

questions.text: Which nerves deliver preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to the inferior hypogastric plexus?
questions.explanation: The pelvic splanchnic nerves arise from S2–S4. They join sympathetic contributions to the mixed inferior hypogastric plexus.

questions.text: Which part of the urinary bladder is most fixed in position?
questions.explanation: The bladder neck is continuous with the urethra and held by condensations of extraperitoneal tissue. The superior surface changes position as the bladder fills.

questions.text: In which part of the uterine tube does fertilization usually occur?
questions.explanation: The ampulla is the widest and longest part of the tube and the usual site of fertilization. The infundibulum is the funnel-shaped distal segment.
options: Intramural segment in the uterine wall

questions.text: Which peritoneal fold conveys the ovarian vessels from the lateral pelvic wall toward the ovary?
questions.explanation: The ovarian vessels enter the pelvis in the suspensory ligament of the ovary and reach the ovarian hilum through the mesovarium. The suspensory ligament is the infundibulopelvic part of the broad ligament in the course description.

questions.text: Which nerve carries somatic pain sensation from the distal vaginal region?
questions.explanation: The distal pain-sensitive region receives somatic sensation through pudendal branches. The upper vagina instead receives autonomic innervation through the uterovaginal plexus.

questions.text: Which lymph nodes first receive most lymph from the skin of the scrotum?
questions.explanation: Cutaneous scrotal lymph drains to superficial inguinal nodes. The testes have a separate route along the testicular vessels to aortic nodes.

questions.text: Which branch of the inferior epigastric artery contributes to the blood supply of the scrotal coverings?
questions.explanation: The inferior epigastric artery supplies the cremasteric artery. The external pudendal arteries arise from the femoral artery and posterior scrotal branches come from the internal pudendal circulation.

questions.text: Which abdominal wall layer gives rise to the internal spermatic fascia?
questions.explanation: The internal spermatic fascia derives from the transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring. The external spermatic fascia comes from external oblique aponeurosis, and the cremasteric layer comes from internal oblique.

questions.text: In which anatomical zone does benign prostatic hyperplasia usually develop?
questions.explanation: Benign hyperplasia usually develops in the transition zone near the prostatic urethra. The question uses zonal anatomy, which is distinct from the classic description of prostatic lobes.

questions.text: In which anatomical zone do most prostate adenocarcinomas arise?
questions.explanation: Most prostatic adenocarcinomas begin in the peripheral zone, which contains the main prostatic acini. Benign hyperplasia usually develops in the transition zone.

questions.text: Where is pararenal fat located relative to the renal fascia?
questions.explanation: Pararenal fat lies outside the renal fascia, predominantly posteriorly in the course description. Perirenal fat lies inside the fascia around the kidney.
options: Between the fibrous capsule and kidney
Within the fascia around the kidney

questions.text: In the textbook model, which direction can fluid track along the opening of the renal fascia?
questions.explanation: The course depicts the renal fascia as remaining open inferiorly along the ureter, allowing perirenal fluid to track toward the pelvis. The question asks about that specific fascial pathway.
options: Medially across to the other kidney

questions.text: A rupture of the spongy urethra breaches its coverings below the perineal membrane. Which perineal space first receives the extravasated urine?
questions.explanation: The spongy urethra lies beneath the perineal membrane. Once its coverings are breached, urine can enter the superficial perineal pouch.

questions.text: Near which vertebral level does the course textbook place the origin of the renal arteries?
questions.explanation: In the course description, the paired renal arteries arise from the sides of the abdominal aorta opposite the upper border of L2.

questions.text: Where do the medial anterior fibres called levator prostatae or pubovaginalis insert?
questions.explanation: These medial fibres pass around the prostate or vagina and insert into the perineal body. Other levator ani subdivisions attach more posteriorly.

questions.text: Which parietal artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery in the course description?
questions.explanation: The inferior gluteal artery is a branch of the anterior division. The superior gluteal, lateral sacral, and iliolumbar branches are assigned to the posterior division.

questions.text: Which branch of the perineal artery supplies the skin of the posterior scrotum?
questions.explanation: The perineal artery gives posterior scrotal branches to the skin of the scrotum. The other listed arteries arise separately from the internal pudendal artery in the course description.
options: Deep artery of the corpus cavernosum

questions.text: List the three main factors that help maintain the kidneys in position in the course description.
questions.explanation: Perirenal fat cushions the kidney within the renal fascia. Neighboring structures and intra-abdominal pressure help maintain its position.
questions.modelAnswer: Perirenal fat, support from adjacent organs, and intra-abdominal pressure.

questions.text: Describe the changes in shape, position, arterial supply and rotation of the developing kidneys.
questions.explanation: Shape, ascent, changing arterial supply and rotation are separate developmental changes. Persistence of lower vessels can account for accessory arterial supply.
questions.modelAnswer: Fetal lobulation is visible at birth and ordinarily disappears during infancy. The kidneys rise from the pelvis to the abdomen with differential growth. They receive successive arterial branches at higher levels during ascent and lower vessels usually regress. The hila rotate from facing anteriorly to facing medially.

questions.text: Name the three main branches of the pudendal nerve in the course description.
questions.explanation: The inferior rectal branch supplies the external anal sphincter and adjacent sensation. The perineal and dorsal branches supply perineal structures and external genital sensation.
questions.modelAnswer: Inferior rectal nerve, perineal nerve, and dorsal nerve of the penis or clitoris.

questions.text: List the six branches of the internal pudendal artery described in the course.
questions.explanation: The artery gives perineal and erectile-tissue branches. Posterior scrotal or labial arteries are branches of the perineal artery and are not additional direct branches in this list.
questions.modelAnswer: Inferior rectal artery, perineal artery, artery to the bulb, urethral artery, deep artery of the penis or clitoris, and dorsal artery of the penis or clitoris.

questions.text: List the lateral relations of the lower, middle and upper parts of the vagina in the course description.
questions.explanation: The lower relations are perineal. The middle relations are to the pelvic floor and the upper relation is to the lateral cervical support.
questions.modelAnswer: Lower part: greater vestibular glands, bulbs of the vestibule, and the muscles termed the urogenital diaphragm in the textbook. Middle part: pubovaginalis fibres of levator ani. Upper part: attachment of the transverse cervical (Mackenrodt) ligament.

questions.text: Where does lymph from the vagina drain above and below the hymen in the course description?
questions.explanation: The course distinguishes distal perineal drainage to superficial inguinal nodes from pelvic drainage of the more proximal vagina.
questions.modelAnswer: Below the hymen: superficial inguinal nodes. Above the hymen: internal and external iliac nodes.

questions.text: From which epithelium do the primary sex cords of the indifferent gonad arise?
questions.explanation: Surface epithelial cells grow into the underlying mesoderm to form solid cords. Primordial germ cells migrate into the gonadal region separately.
questions.modelAnswer: Proliferating coelomic epithelium covering the genital ridge.

questions.text: By which month is the vaginal plate completely canalized in the designated textbook's account?
questions.explanation: The paired sinovaginal bulbs unite to form the solid vaginal plate, which subsequently canalizes. The course textbook gives completion by the fifth month.
questions.modelAnswer: By the end of the fifth month of development.

questions.text: List the branches of the internal iliac artery by division. Separate anterior parietal and visceral branches.
questions.explanation: The posterior division supplies the body wall in the course classification. The anterior division gives both body-wall and pelvic-organ branches, including sex-specific visceral branches.
questions.modelAnswer: Posterior division: iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal. Anterior parietal: obturator, internal pudendal and inferior gluteal. Anterior visceral: umbilical with superior vesical branches, middle rectal, inferior vesical in the male or vaginal in the female, and uterine in the female.

questions.text: Describe the apex, base, and four walls of the ischioanal fossa.
questions.explanation: The fossa is a wedge-shaped space beside the anal canal. Its walls explain the lateral position of the pudendal canal and the medial course of the inferior rectal neurovascular bundle.
questions.modelAnswer: Apex: junction of obturator internus and levator ani. Base: perianal skin. Medial wall: levator ani and external anal sphincter. Lateral wall: obturator internus with its fascia and the ischial tuberosity. Anterior boundary: posterior border of the perineal membrane and adjacent posterior urogenital triangle muscles. Posterior boundary: sacrotuberous ligament and lower border of gluteus maximus.

questions.text: List the main contents of the ischioanal fossa and specify which neurovascular structures lie in its lateral-wall canal.
questions.explanation: The fat allows expansion of the anal canal. The inferior rectal bundle crosses the fossa, while the main pudendal structures are contained within the lateral wall's fascial canal.
questions.modelAnswer: Fat fills the fossa. Inferior rectal nerves and vessels cross it medially. The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels lie within the pudendal canal along the lateral wall.

questions.text: Name the arteries supplying the testis and epididymis and trace testicular venous drainage on each side.
questions.explanation: The pampiniform plexus merges into the testicular vein proximally. Its termination differs on the two sides.
questions.modelAnswer: The testicular, cremasteric and deferential arteries contribute. Veins form the pampiniform plexus and unite as the testicular vein. The right testicular vein enters the inferior vena cava and the left enters the left renal vein.

questions.text: Name the arterial sources of the prostate and trace its main venous drainage.
questions.explanation: The prostatic venous plexus communicates with the vesical plexus. The requested drainage endpoint is the internal iliac veins.
questions.modelAnswer: Arterial supply comes from branches of the inferior vesical, internal pudendal and middle rectal arteries. Veins form the prostatic venous plexus, which drains into the internal iliac veins.

questions.text: List four arterial sources of the breast in the course description.
questions.explanation: The breast receives contributions from both thoracic wall and axillary arterial routes.
questions.modelAnswer: Mammary branches of the lateral thoracic and thoracoacromial arteries, perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery, and lateral branches of posterior intercostal arteries.

questions.text: What is the usual anterior-to-posterior order of the major structures at the renal hilum?
questions.explanation: The major structures are arranged vein, artery and pelvis from front to back. Smaller vessels and nerves also pass through the hilum.
options: Renal artery, renal pelvis, renal vein
Renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis
Renal pelvis, renal vein, renal artery
Renal vein, renal pelvis, renal artery

questions.text: From the kidney surface outward, what is the usual order of the three innermost coverings?
questions.explanation: The fibrous capsule adheres to the kidney. Perirenal fat sits around it inside the renal fascia. Pararenal fat lies outside that fascia.
options: Renal fascia, fibrous capsule, perirenal fat
Perirenal fat, fibrous capsule, renal fascia
Fibrous capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia
Perirenal fat, renal fascia, fibrous capsule

questions.text: Which term names a segment of the male urethra rather than a part of the ureter?
questions.explanation: The ureter has abdominal and pelvic portions and traverses the bladder wall in its intramural course. The membranous segment belongs to the male urethra.

questions.text: Which site is the narrowest point of the male urethra when the external outlet is included?
questions.explanation: The external urethral meatus is the narrowest point overall. The membranous segment is the narrowest segment when the external meatus is excluded, and it is relatively nondistensible.

questions.text: What do the urethral glands of Littre primarily secrete?
questions.explanation: Glands of Littre secrete mucus that lubricates the urethral lining. Their secretory role differs from that of the prostate and seminal vesicles.

questions.text: Which structure receives urine directly as it exits the renal papillary ducts?
questions.explanation: Papillary ducts open at the tip of a renal papilla and empty into a minor calyx. Urine then travels to a major calyx, the renal pelvis and the ureter.

questions.text: In the conventional model, which artery limits the ascent of a horseshoe kidney by meeting the fused isthmus?
questions.explanation: The teaching model places the fused isthmus below the inferior mesenteric artery, leaving the horseshoe kidney lower than the usual renal position.

questions.text: Describe how to mark the Morris rectangle for the posterior surface projection of a kidney.
questions.explanation: The reference is a four-sided rectangle or parallelogram. Its two vertical distances and two spinous-process levels define the projection in this course.
questions.modelAnswer: Draw two vertical lines 1 inch and 3 inches from the midline on the relevant side. Draw the horizontal limits at the tips of the spinous processes of T11 and L3.

questions.text: Name the principal arterial sources of the abdominal and pelvic ureter in the course description.
questions.explanation: A longitudinal arterial network receives contributions along the abdominal course. The distal pelvic network draws from adjacent pelvic arteries, with the named sex-specific contributions.
questions.modelAnswer: Abdominal ureter: branches of renal and gonadal arteries, the abdominal aorta and common iliac artery. Pelvic ureter: contributions from the inferior vesical artery in males, and vaginal and uterine arteries in females.

questions.text: Describe the surface projection line of the ureter in the course diagram.
questions.explanation: The diagram uses one upper surface point and a lower palpable landmark to approximate the course. This is a surface projection.
questions.modelAnswer: A line from a point on the transpyloric plane about 5 cm from the midline to the pubic tubercle on the same side.

questions.text: Name the principal arteries supplying the urinary bladder in males and females and trace the main venous outflow.
questions.explanation: The bladder receives several pelvic arterial contributions. Its principal vesical outflow terminates in the internal iliac veins.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior vesical arteries contribute in both sexes. Inferior vesical arteries are the usual additional named source in males, and vaginal arteries in females. Vesical veins drain from the vesical venous plexus to internal iliac veins.

questions.text: Which three branches does the course textbook list as arising from the dorsal surface of the sacral plexus?
questions.explanation: The textbook lists these separately from branches arising from the roots, ventral surface, or both plexus surfaces.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior gluteal nerve, inferior gluteal nerve and perforating cutaneous nerve.

questions.text: Name the direct branches of the internal pudendal artery in the female in the course description.
questions.explanation: The list uses the corresponding female erectile structures. Posterior labial arteries are branches of the perineal artery in the course description.
questions.modelAnswer: Inferior rectal artery, perineal artery, artery to the bulb of the vestibule, urethral artery, and deep and dorsal arteries of the clitoris.

questions.text: Describe the boundaries and principal contents of the male superficial perineal pouch in the course model.
questions.explanation: The perineal membrane separates this pouch from the deeper space. The superficial fascial boundaries explain its anterior continuity and posterior limit.
questions.modelAnswer: Roof: perineal membrane. Floor: membranous superficial perineal fascia. Laterally: attached at the pubic arch. Posteriorly: closed where the fascia fuses with the posterior border of the perineal membrane. Anteriorly: continuous with the plane under membranous superficial fascia of the lower abdominal wall. Principal contents include penile crura and bulb, proximal spongy urethra, bulbourethral gland ducts, ischiocavernosus, bulbospongiosus and superficial transverse perineal muscles, and associated perineal vessels and nerves.

questions.text: Describe the boundaries and principal contents of the female deep perineal pouch in the course model.
questions.explanation: The perineal membrane separates the deep pouch from the superficial pouch in the course model. The urethra and vagina traverse the female deep space.
questions.modelAnswer: Floor: perineal membrane. Roof: superior fascia of the urogenital diaphragm. Lateral limits: ischiopubic rami. The fasciae fuse at the anterior and posterior limits in the course model. Principal contents include parts of urethra and vagina, the external urethral sphincter complex, deep transverse perineal muscles, terminal internal pudendal vessels and the dorsal nerve of the clitoris.

questions.text: Which cutaneous nerves supply the posterior two-thirds of the scrotum in the course description?
questions.explanation: Posterior scrotal skin has contributions from both paths. Ilioinguinal and genital branch of genitofemoral supply the anterior region.
questions.modelAnswer: Posterior scrotal branches of the perineal nerve from the pudendal nerve, and the perineal branch of the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve.

questions.text: Which two anterior contacts of the right kidney face peritoneum-covered areas in the course description?
questions.explanation: The course distinguishes these peritoneal areas from the parts directly related to the suprarenal gland, duodenum and right colic flexure.
questions.modelAnswer: The right lobe of the liver and loops of small intestine.

questions.text: Compare the main superior relations of the urinary bladder in a male and female with the bladder empty.
questions.explanation: Peritoneum covers the superior bladder. Its posterior reflection differs between the two sexes, and the uterus changes the relations in the female pelvis.
questions.modelAnswer: The superior surface is covered by peritoneum. In the male it is related to loops of ileum or sigmoid colon. In the female it is related to the uterus, with the uterovesical peritoneal reflection between them, and bowel loops can intervene.

questions.text: After a straddle injury, urine has leaked into the superficial perineal pouch and extended into the lower anterior abdominal wall. The swelling does not track down the thighs.
questions.explanation: The distribution follows the continuous superficial perineal and lower abdominal fascial planes. The case tests the injured urethral segment, the fascial limit and where superficial fluid can spread.
questions.modelAnswer: The distribution follows the continuous superficial perineal and lower abdominal fascial planes. The case tests the injured urethral segment, the fascial limit and where superficial fluid can spread.

subQuestions.text: Which urethral segment below the perineal membrane is consistent with this pattern?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The spongy urethra, classically in the bulbar region after a straddle injury.
subQuestions.explanation: The proximal spongy urethra lies in the superficial perineal region below the membrane.

subQuestions.text: Which fascial attachment limits inferior spread into the thigh?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The membranous superficial fascia of the lower abdominal wall, or Scarpa fascia, attaches to fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament.
subQuestions.explanation: That junction closes the superficial plane toward the thigh. Scarpa fascia is a membranous layer of superficial fascia.

subQuestions.text: Name two other external regions where the fluid can spread in this superficial fascial plane.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The scrotum and the superficial tissues of the penis.
subQuestions.explanation: These regions communicate with the superficial perineal fascial plane.

questions.text: Compare two developmental findings in infants. In the first, a testis remains in the inguinal canal. In the second, a testis is located at the root of the penis.
questions.explanation: The first location lies along the normal descent pathway. The second lies outside that route and illustrates ectopic descent.
questions.modelAnswer: The first location lies along the normal descent pathway. The second lies outside that route and illustrates ectopic descent.

subQuestions.text: Classify each finding by its relationship to the normal descent pathway.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: An inguinal testis arrested along the normal route is undescended. A testis at the root of the penis lies off that route and is ectopic.
subQuestions.explanation: The distinction is the testis's proven location relative to the normal path.

subQuestions.text: How can abnormal gubernacular attachment contribute to ectopic descent in the course account?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The gubernaculum normally helps guide descent toward the scrotum. An abnormal gubernacular attachment can guide the testis to a site outside the normal route.
subQuestions.explanation: Abnormal guidance is distinct from arrest along the usual route.

subQuestions.text: Name two other ectopic sites listed in the course.
subQuestions.explanation: Each lies outside the normal ipsilateral route to the scrotum.

questions.text: Which skeletal muscle covers each crus of the penis?
questions.explanation: Ischiocavernosus covers each crus. Bulbospongiosus instead lies over the bulb of the penis.

questions.text: Which adult structure derives from the distal remnant of the processus vaginalis?
questions.explanation: The proximal processus vaginalis normally obliterates, and the distal serous remnant persists as the tunica vaginalis around part of the testis.

questions.text: Which opening connects the uterine cavity to the cervical canal?
questions.explanation: The internal os lies at the junction of uterine cavity and cervical canal. The external os opens from the cervical canal into the vagina.
options: Abdominal ostium of the uterine tube

questions.text: Which nodes receive lymph from the part of the vagina below the hymen in the course description?
questions.explanation: The distal region below the hymen is described as draining to superficial inguinal nodes. The more proximal vagina drains to pelvic lymph nodes.

questions.text: From which vessel does the ovarian artery typically arise?
questions.explanation: The ovarian artery usually arises from the abdominal aorta and descends toward the ovary in the suspensory ligament.
options: Anterior division of internal iliac artery
Posterior division of internal iliac artery

questions.text: Which term refers collectively to the external female genitalia?
questions.explanation: The vulva includes the labia, clitoris, vestibule and other external genital structures. The vestibule is one component of this region.

questions.text: Which part of the broad ligament extends from the lateral side of the uterus toward the pelvic wall below the ovary?
questions.explanation: The mesometrium is the broad uterine part of the ligament below the ovary and its ligament. The mesosalpinx relates to the uterine tube and the mesovarium attaches to the ovary.

questions.text: From the lateral breast, which lymph node group usually receives the principal drainage first in the course description?
questions.explanation: Lymph from the lateral breast usually reaches the anterior or pectoral axillary nodes. The medial breast also has an important parasternal drainage route.
options: Parasternal nodes along the internal thoracic vessels

questions.text: Which plane allows the breast to move over the pectoral fascia?
questions.explanation: The retromammary space is a loose connective-tissue plane between the breast and pectoral fascia. It permits movement over pectoralis major.
options: Plane between pectoralis major and minor

questions.text: What is the name of the circular area of pigmented skin around the nipple?
questions.explanation: The areola surrounds the nipple and contains areolar glands. The axillary tail is a superolateral extension of breast tissue.

questions.text: Which landmarks define the imaginary line separating the urogenital and anal triangles?
questions.explanation: The transverse line joining the ischial tuberosities divides the perineum into the anterior urogenital and posterior anal triangles.
options: The right and left anterior superior iliac spines
The pubic symphysis and tip of the coccyx

questions.text: Which ribs normally have a posterior relation to the left kidney in the course description?
questions.explanation: The left kidney lies higher than the right. It relates posteriorly through the diaphragm to the eleventh and twelfth ribs, while the right usually relates to the twelfth rib.

questions.text: Which of these nerves arises from the sacral plexus?
questions.explanation: The pudendal nerve arises from S2–S4 of the sacral plexus. The other listed nerves arise from the lumbar plexus.

questions.text: Where do the deep arteries of the penis run after entering the crura?
questions.explanation: The deep penile arteries enter the crura and run within the corpora cavernosa, where their branches supply the erectile spaces.

questions.text: Which structure is a remnant of the cranial end of the paramesonephric duct in the male?
questions.explanation: The appendix testis is a cranial paramesonephric remnant. The appendix epididymis and male ductal structures listed here derive from the mesonephric system.

questions.text: Through which opening does the superior gluteal artery leave the pelvis?
questions.explanation: The superior gluteal artery leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, above piriformis.

questions.text: While sitting upright, which bony landmarks directly support the weight of the trunk?
questions.explanation: Weight is transmitted to the seat through the ischial tuberosities. The ischial spines project into the pelvis and lie superior to the tuberosities.

questions.text: Which named fibres of levator ani pass beside the vagina and attach to the perineal body?
questions.explanation: The pubovaginalis fibres pass along the vaginal wall to the perineal body. The puborectalis forms a sling around the anorectal junction, and iliococcygeus attaches posteriorly to the coccyx and anococcygeal raphe.

questions.text: Which muscle forms a U-shaped sling around the anorectal junction and helps maintain the anorectal angle?
questions.explanation: Puborectalis loops behind the anorectal junction and pulls it forward. The external anal sphincter surrounds the anal canal but is distinct from this sling.

questions.text: Which artery passes between the lumbosacral trunk and the S1 ventral ramus as it leaves the pelvis?
questions.explanation: The superior gluteal artery travels between the lumbosacral trunk and the S1 ventral ramus and exits above piriformis. The inferior gluteal artery exits below piriformis.

questions.text: Which artery typically arises from the posterior division of the internal iliac artery?
questions.explanation: The iliolumbar artery normally comes from the posterior division. The other listed arteries are usual anterior division branches.

questions.text: The deep arteries that supply the erectile tissue of the corpora cavernosa are branches of which artery?
questions.explanation: The internal pudendal artery supplies the penis through branches including the deep and dorsal penile arteries. The deep arteries supply the cavernosal erectile tissue.

questions.text: Which structures lie immediately anterior and posterior, respectively, to the seminal vesicles?
questions.explanation: The seminal vesicles lie behind the base of the bladder and in front of the rectum. They are superior to the prostate.

questions.text: Which of these arteries contributes to the blood supply of the seminal vesicles?
questions.explanation: The seminal vesicles receive branches from the middle rectal and inferior vesical arteries.

questions.text: Which structure directly contacts the base of the prostate?
questions.explanation: The base is the upper surface of the prostate. It supports the bladder neck as the urethra passes from the bladder into the gland.
options: Inferior surface of the bladder body

questions.text: Which vein directly receives the left testicular vein?
questions.explanation: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein. The right testicular vein normally drains directly into the inferior vena cava.

questions.text: The posterior scrotal nerves arise from the perineal branch of which nerve?
questions.explanation: Posterior scrotal branches arise from the perineal branch of the pudendal nerve. A perineal branch of the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve also contributes to sensation in the area.

questions.text: A male newborn has a red mucosal plate on the lower anterior abdominal wall just above the pubis. Urine dribbles onto the exposed surface.
questions.explanation: The findings describe bladder exstrophy and its associated urethral anomaly.
questions.modelAnswer: The findings describe bladder exstrophy and its associated urethral anomaly.

subQuestions.text: Identify the anomaly and give its embryological cause in the course account.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Bladder exstrophy (ectopia vesicae). Deficient development of the ventral abdominal wall is followed by rupture of the overlying membrane, leaving the anterior bladder wall and overlying abdominal wall deficient and the bladder mucosa exposed.
subQuestions.explanation: The exposed mucosa and urine drainage distinguish bladder exstrophy from an umbilical urachal fistula.

subQuestions.text: Name the associated anomaly of the urethra in the external genitalia.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Epispadias, with the urethra opening on the dorsal aspect of the penis.
subQuestions.explanation: The course illustration identifies epispadias as the associated urethral defect.

questions.text: Which of these is a visceral branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery?
questions.explanation: The uterine artery supplies pelvic viscera. The obturator is a parietal branch, the lateral sacral is from the posterior division, and the superior rectal is the continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery.

questions.text: Which part of levator ani arises near the ischial spine and inserts into the anococcygeal raphe?
questions.explanation: Iliococcygeus arises from the posterior part of the tendinous arch and adjacent ischial spine. It inserts into the anococcygeal raphe and side of the coccyx. Pubococcygeus proper also reaches the raphe but arises more anteriorly.

questions.text: Which ventral rami normally contribute to the pudendal nerve?
questions.explanation: The pudendal nerve arises from the S2–S4 ventral rami of the sacral plexus.

questions.text: To which bony structures are the lateral margins of the perineal membrane attached?
questions.explanation: The membrane spans the urogenital triangle between the ischiopubic rami. Its posterior margin is connected to the perineal body.
options: Roots of the superior pubic rami

questions.text: Which structure is a content of the male deep perineal pouch?
questions.explanation: The bulbourethral glands lie in the deep pouch. Their ducts pass through the perineal membrane and open into the spongy urethra.

questions.text: A 16-year-old girl has clear, urine-smelling discharge from her umbilicus when she coughs or sneezes. No umbilical swelling is visible.
questions.explanation: The case tests patency of the urachus, its normal adult remnant and other patterns of incomplete obliteration.
questions.modelAnswer: The case tests patency of the urachus, its normal adult remnant and other patterns of incomplete obliteration.

subQuestions.text: Identify the anomaly that explains the discharge.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: A patent urachus (urachal fistula) connecting the bladder apex and the umbilicus.
subQuestions.explanation: A completely patent tract can conduct urine from the bladder to the umbilicus.

subQuestions.text: What is the normal adult remnant of the urachus?
subQuestions.explanation: The urachal lumen normally obliterates, leaving a fibrous ligament between the bladder apex and umbilicus.

subQuestions.text: Name two other patterns of incomplete urachal obliteration.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: A urachal cyst, where a central segment stays patent, and an umbilical urachal sinus, where the umbilical end remains open and ends blindly.
subQuestions.explanation: A cyst has no open connection at either end. An umbilical sinus opens only at the umbilical end; a vesicourachal diverticulum is another valid example, opening only to the bladder.

questions.text: Which embryonic tissue forms the epithelium of Bowman’s capsule?
questions.explanation: Metanephric cap mesenchyme forms the nephron epithelium, including the capsule. The ureteric bud forms the collecting system.

questions.text: Which ducts open into the prostatic sinuses on either side of the urethral crest?
questions.explanation: The prostatic ductules empty into the prostatic sinuses. The ejaculatory ducts open separately near the prostatic utricle on the seminal colliculus.

questions.text: Which transverse surface landmark usually lies just above the right renal hilum and just below the left renal hilum?
questions.explanation: The transpyloric plane passes at about L1. The right kidney sits slightly lower than the left, so the right hilum lies just below the plane and the left hilum just above it.
