questions.text: List the main microscopic structures present in the renal cortex.
questions.explanation: The renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules are part of the cortical labyrinth. The medullary rays are bundles of straight tubules within the cortex.
questions.modelAnswer: Renal corpuscles, proximal and distal convoluted tubules, cortical peritubular capillaries, and medullary rays. The rays contain straight tubular segments and collecting ducts.

questions.text: List the main tubular and vascular structures in the renal medulla.
questions.explanation: The tubules and vessels run through the medullary pyramids. Renal corpuscles are restricted to the cortex.
questions.modelAnswer: Loops of Henle, collecting ducts, and medullary capillaries including the vasa recta.

questions.text: Explain how features of the renal cortex and medulla interdigitate.
questions.explanation: The columns and rays extend in opposite directions across the overall corticomedullary interface.
questions.modelAnswer: Renal columns are inward extensions of cortical tissue between adjacent medullary pyramids. Medullary rays are bundles of straight tubules and collecting ducts extending from the pyramids into the cortex.

questions.text: List the two main components of a uriniferous tubule and name the parts of its nephron.
questions.explanation: Filtration begins in the renal corpuscle. Filtrate passes through the nephron tubules before entering the collecting system.
questions.modelAnswer: A uriniferous tubule consists of a nephron and a collecting tubule. The nephron comprises the renal corpuscle, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, and distal tubule.

questions.text: Name the components of the renal corpuscle, including the structures that make up the glomerulus.
questions.explanation: The visceral and parietal layers of Bowman’s capsule enclose a urinary space that receives filtrate from the glomerular capillaries.
questions.modelAnswer: The renal corpuscle consists of Bowman’s capsule and the glomerulus. The glomerulus comprises a capillary tuft and associated mesangium.

questions.text: Describe the cell body, processes and filtration slits of a podocyte on electron microscopy.
questions.explanation: The foot processes of neighboring podocytes interdigitate. Their slits form the epithelial part of the filtration barrier.
questions.modelAnswer: A podocyte has a flattened cell body with an irregular nucleus. Primary processes curve around the capillaries and branch into interdigitating foot processes that contact the glomerular basement membrane. A slit diaphragm spans each slit between adjacent foot processes.

questions.text: Describe how the glomerular basement membrane forms and name its three conventional electron-microscopic layers from endothelium to podocyte.
questions.explanation: The shared basement membrane lies between fenestrated capillary endothelium and the podocyte foot processes.
questions.modelAnswer: It forms from the fused basal laminae of glomerular endothelial cells and podocytes. From the endothelium outward are the electron-lucent lamina rara interna, electron-dense lamina densa, and electron-lucent lamina rara externa adjacent to podocytes.

questions.text: List the layers of the glomerular filtration barrier from capillary blood to Bowman space.
questions.explanation: Filtrate passes from the capillary lumen across the endothelium, basement membrane and epithelial slit diaphragms before entering Bowman space.
questions.modelAnswer: Fenestrated glomerular capillary endothelium, the shared glomerular basement membrane, and the podocyte foot-process slits spanned by slit diaphragms.

questions.text: Describe four functions of intraglomerular mesangial cells.
questions.explanation: These cells occupy spaces between glomerular capillary loops. Their supporting, phagocytic and contractile roles differ from those of podocytes.
questions.modelAnswer: They provide structural support for capillary loops, synthesize and remodel mesangial matrix, clear trapped material by phagocytosis, and contract to regulate the capillary surface available for filtration. They can also release signaling mediators such as cytokines and prostaglandins.

questions.text: Compare the epithelial cells and lumen of proximal and distal convoluted tubules on a routine renal section.
questions.explanation: The brush border makes the proximal lumen look fuzzy. A distal tubule of comparable section size usually shows more nuclei around its lumen.
questions.modelAnswer: The proximal tubule has taller, more eosinophilic cuboidal cells, a prominent brush border, indistinct cell boundaries and a less clearly defined lumen. The distal tubule has lower, paler cuboidal cells, sparse microvilli, clearer cell boundaries and an open, well-defined lumen.

questions.text: From proximal to distal, name the thick and thin segments of the loop of Henle in a long-loop nephron.
questions.explanation: Long juxtamedullary loops include a thin ascending segment. A short cortical loop may lack this segment.
questions.modelAnswer: Thick descending segment (the straight proximal tubule), thin descending limb, thin ascending limb, and thick ascending limb.

questions.text: What is the loop of Henle’s role in creating the medullary osmotic gradient?
questions.explanation: The gradient allows water reabsorption from collecting ducts when their water permeability increases. Vasa recta help preserve it.
questions.modelAnswer: The loop acts as a countercurrent multiplier. The ascending limb removes sodium chloride with little water, while the descending limb allows water to leave. This creates and amplifies the medullary osmotic gradient.

questions.text: Describe a cortical collecting-duct principal cell under electron microscopy.
questions.explanation: ADH promotes insertion of aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane and increases water permeability.
questions.modelAnswer: It has sparse apical microvilli and a primary cilium, aquaporin-containing subapical vesicles, relatively few mitochondria, limited lateral interdigitation and basal membrane infoldings.

questions.text: How do type A and type B intercalated cells contribute to acid–base balance?
questions.explanation: The two cell types place their major transport proteins on different membrane surfaces, allowing opposite handling of bicarbonate.
questions.modelAnswer: Type A cells secrete hydrogen ions into tubular fluid and return bicarbonate to blood. Type B cells can secrete bicarbonate into tubular fluid.

questions.text: Describe the position and microscopic features of macula densa cells.
questions.explanation: The macula densa senses tubular sodium chloride delivery and signals to adjacent cells in the juxtaglomerular apparatus.
questions.modelAnswer: They form a closely packed patch of specialized distal tubular epithelial cells at the vascular pole of a renal corpuscle. Their crowded nuclei are prominent. In the course description they have apical microvilli, sparse basal infoldings and a Golgi apparatus basal to the nucleus.

questions.text: Why do umbrella cells of the urothelium have tight junctions near their apical surfaces?
questions.explanation: Uroplakin plaques contribute to membrane impermeability. The tight junctions restrict movement between adjacent cells.
questions.modelAnswer: The tight junctions restrict paracellular movement of water and solutes. Together with the low-permeability apical membrane, they help maintain the barrier between urine and tissue fluid.

questions.text: Compare the smooth muscle layers in the upper two-thirds and lower third of the ureter.
questions.explanation: The muscle coat generates peristaltic contractions that propel urine toward the bladder.
questions.modelAnswer: The upper two-thirds has inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle. The lower third has inner longitudinal, middle circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle.

questions.text: List the principal coverings of the testis from superficial to deep.
questions.explanation: The vaginalis is a serous covering; the albuginea is the fibrous capsule and the vasculosa is the inner vascular layer.
questions.modelAnswer: Tunica vaginalis, tunica albuginea and tunica vasculosa.

questions.text: What are two functions of the peritubular myoid cells around seminiferous tubules?
questions.explanation: The contractile cells lie in the tissue around the seminiferous epithelium.
questions.modelAnswer: They contract to help propel luminal contents, including spermatozoa, along the tubules. They also synthesize extracellular matrix, including collagen.

questions.text: Why do cytoplasmic bridges persist between developing male germ cells?
questions.explanation: Nuclear division can finish while final separation of the daughter cells remains incomplete.
questions.modelAnswer: Cytokinesis is incomplete during divisions of differentiating germ cells. The daughter cells retain cytoplasmic connections.

questions.text: What do cytoplasmic bridges allow developing male germ cells in a clone to do?
questions.explanation: These connections coordinate cohorts of differentiating germ cells.
questions.modelAnswer: They allow exchange of cytoplasmic products and help synchronize development. Haploid cells can share products of genes that are not present in each cell.

questions.text: Name the three acrosomal enzymes listed in the course and describe their overall role in fertilization.
questions.explanation: The enzymes act together with sperm motility and surface interactions. No one enzyme alone explains penetration.
questions.modelAnswer: Hyaluronidase, acrosin and acid phosphatase. Acrosomal contents participate in sperm passage through the investments around the secondary oocyte, including the cumulus and zona pellucida.

questions.text: How does the axoneme generate bending of the sperm flagellum?
questions.explanation: The dynein motors are part of the axoneme; the outer dense fibers support the tail.
questions.modelAnswer: Dynein motors hydrolyze ATP and drive sliding of adjacent microtubule doublets. Constraints on the doublets convert relative sliding into bending along the flagellum.

questions.text: Why can Kartagener syndrome reduce male fertility and cause recurrent respiratory infections?
questions.explanation: The sperm flagellum and motile respiratory cilia use related axonemal machinery. Defects in that machinery can affect both systems.
questions.modelAnswer: Impaired motile cilia and flagella reduce sperm motility and weaken mucociliary clearance in the airways. The first can reduce fertility; the second promotes retention of mucus and recurrent infection.

questions.text: Trace the duct sequence from the seminiferous tubules to the epididymal duct.
questions.explanation: The efferent ductules traverse the testicular covering, so the sequence identifies them more precisely than a broad regional label.
questions.modelAnswer: Seminiferous tubules drain into straight tubules (tubuli recti), then the rete testis, and then efferent ductules that lead to the head of the epididymis.

questions.text: How do efferent ductules move sperm and modify the fluid entering the epididymis?
questions.explanation: These functions characterize the efferent ductules. The same epithelial arrangement is not present throughout the outflow tract.
questions.modelAnswer: Ciliary beating and smooth-muscle contractions help transport sperm toward the epididymal duct. Nonciliated absorptive cells reabsorb much of the testicular fluid.

questions.text: Describe the lining epithelium of the epididymal duct and name its main cell types.
questions.explanation: Stereocilia here are long nonmotile microvilli that increase apical surface area.
questions.modelAnswer: It is pseudostratified columnar epithelium. Tall principal cells bear stereocilia and smaller basal cells rest near the basement membrane.

questions.text: What functional and membrane changes occur as sperm mature in the epididymis?
questions.explanation: These are maturation changes. Capacitation happens later after sperm leave the epididymis.
questions.modelAnswer: Sperm acquire the capacity for progressive motility. Their surface membrane changes, including changes in lipid and protein composition that regulate the acrosomal response.

questions.text: Name the smooth muscle layers of the ductus deferens from lumen outward.
questions.explanation: The three thick layers generate strong contractions that help propel sperm during emission.
questions.modelAnswer: Inner longitudinal, middle circular and outer longitudinal.

questions.text: Name the smooth muscle layers of the seminal vesicle from inside outward.
questions.explanation: The muscle contracts to expel secretion. It lies outside the folded mucosa.
questions.modelAnswer: Inner circular and outer longitudinal.

questions.text: In the course’s acinar classification of the prostate, name the three groups and state how their ducts reach the urethra.
questions.explanation: The classification concerns groups of prostatic acini and their ducts. The urethral lining is a separate structure.
questions.modelAnswer: The groups are mucosal, submucosal and main. Mucosal acini drain through short ducts directly into the prostatic urethral lumen. Submucosal and main gland ducts take a longer arched course and open at the posterior margin of the prostatic urethra.

questions.text: What epithelial patterns may line the glandular acini of the prostate?
questions.explanation: The acini are secretory units. Their ducts carry secretion to the urethra, whose lining is a separate epithelium.
questions.modelAnswer: The acini can be lined by simple cuboidal, simple columnar or pseudostratified columnar epithelium.

questions.text: Describe prostatic secretion and explain how it acts on semen after ejaculation.
questions.explanation: PSA helps release sperm from the coagulum after ejaculation.
questions.modelAnswer: The prostate contributes a thin milky secretion containing citrate and proteolytic enzymes such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA). These enzymes help liquefy the seminal coagulum.

questions.text: In which prostate zone does benign prostatic hyperplasia usually arise, and in which zone do most prostatic adenocarcinomas arise?
questions.explanation: The transition zone is close to the urethra, so enlargement there can affect urinary outflow.
questions.modelAnswer: BPH usually begins in the transition zone near the proximal urethra. Most prostatic adenocarcinomas arise in the peripheral zone.

questions.text: At what meiotic stage is a primary oocyte arrested, and at what stage is a secondary oocyte arrested?
questions.explanation: The first arrest can persist for years. The second arrest normally ends after fertilization.
questions.modelAnswer: Primary oocyte: diplotene of prophase I. Secondary oocyte: metaphase II.

questions.text: When are meiosis I and meiosis II normally completed during human oocyte development?
questions.explanation: Completion of meiosis I produces the secondary oocyte and first polar body. The secondary oocyte is ovulated during meiosis II.
questions.modelAnswer: Meiosis I completes shortly before ovulation. Meiosis II completes after fertilization triggers resumption of division.

questions.text: What do ovarian hilar cells secrete?
questions.explanation: Hilar cells are steroid-producing cells in the ovarian hilum.
questions.modelAnswer: Androgens.

questions.text: What two features identify a primordial follicle on a histology section?
questions.explanation: A unilaminar primary follicle has cuboidal follicular cells rather than the flattened cells of a primordial follicle.
questions.modelAnswer: It contains a primary oocyte surrounded by a single layer of flattened follicular cells.

questions.text: What role does the zona pellucida play during fertilization?
questions.explanation: The coat participates in sperm–oocyte recognition. Its postfertilization modification helps limit fertilization to one sperm.
questions.modelAnswer: It is a glycoprotein coat around the oocyte that participates in sperm binding. After fertilization, cortical granule release modifies the coat and helps prevent additional sperm from entering.

questions.text: Where do the thecal layers of a growing ovarian follicle come from, and how do the two layers differ?
questions.explanation: Granulosa cells can aromatize the androgens produced by the theca interna.
questions.modelAnswer: The surrounding ovarian stroma condenses to form both layers. The vascular theca interna contains steroidogenic cells that make androgen precursors. The outer theca externa contains fibrous connective tissue and smooth muscle.

questions.text: Name the three regions of granulosa cells in a mature Graafian follicle and state where each lies.
questions.explanation: The corona radiata is part of the cumulus and remains around the ovulated oocyte.
questions.modelAnswer: The mural granulosa lines the follicle wall. The cumulus oophorus is the mound of granulosa cells that surrounds and supports the oocyte. Its innermost layer next to the zona pellucida is the corona radiata.

questions.text: Explain the hormonal trigger for ovulation and how it leads to follicular rupture.
questions.explanation: The LH surge links the estrogen signal from the dominant follicle to its rupture.
questions.modelAnswer: Sustained high estradiol from the dominant follicle switches to positive feedback, inducing the midcycle LH surge. LH promotes oocyte maturation and remodeling of the follicle wall, which ruptures and releases the secondary oocyte.

questions.text: What structure forms from the follicle remaining after ovulation, and what happens to its granulosa and theca interna cells?
questions.explanation: The corpus luteum is a temporary endocrine structure. Regression leaves a corpus albicans.
questions.modelAnswer: The follicle forms the corpus luteum. Granulosa cells become granulosa lutein cells, and theca interna cells become theca lutein cells. Both produce steroids. With luteal regression the structure is replaced by a fibrous corpus albicans.

questions.text: Which trophoblast layer produces hCG, and what does hCG do to the corpus luteum in early pregnancy?
questions.explanation: hCG supports progesterone secretion early in pregnancy. Progesterone helps maintain the endometrium.
questions.modelAnswer: The syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG. It maintains the corpus luteum and its progesterone secretion in early pregnancy as the placenta develops steroid-producing capacity.

questions.text: From which follicular cell population do ovarian interstitial steroidogenic cells originate in the course histology description?
questions.explanation: The steroidogenic cells can persist in the ovarian stroma after the follicle undergoes atresia.
questions.modelAnswer: They originate from theca interna cells of atretic follicles.

questions.text: Summarize the structural events of the follicular, ovulatory and luteal phases of the ovarian cycle.
questions.explanation: The ovarian cycle describes changes in the follicle and corpus luteum.
questions.modelAnswer: In the follicular phase recruited follicles grow and a dominant follicle reaches maturity. At ovulation it ruptures and releases a secondary oocyte. In the luteal phase the residual follicle forms the corpus luteum, which regresses without ongoing support or is maintained early in pregnancy.

questions.text: What hormones do ovarian interstitial steroidogenic cells produce, and how can granulosa cells use these hormones?
questions.explanation: Aromatase activity provides the link between ovarian androgen production and estrogen synthesis.
questions.modelAnswer: Ovarian interstitial steroidogenic cells produce androgens. Granulosa cells can convert androgen substrates to estrogens using aromatase.

questions.text: Describe the lining epithelium of the uterine tube and the function of each of its two main cell types.
questions.explanation: The proportions of these cell types vary with segment and cycle stage.
questions.modelAnswer: It is simple columnar epithelium with ciliated cells and nonciliated secretory cells. Ciliary beating helps transport tubal contents toward the uterus. Secretory cells contribute to the luminal fluid.

questions.text: How does the epithelium of the uterine tube change from the follicular phase to the postovulatory phase?
questions.explanation: The uterine tube epithelium responds to cyclic ovarian hormones.
questions.modelAnswer: In the estrogen-dominant follicular phase epithelial cells become taller and ciliation increases. After ovulation, ciliated cells become shorter relative to the secretory cells, and secretory cells become more prominent.

questions.text: Compare the stratum functionalis and stratum basalis of the endometrium in position, blood supply and fate at menstruation.
questions.explanation: The glands remaining in the basalis help restore the endometrial surface after menstruation.
questions.modelAnswer: The superficial functionalis contains the surface and upper portions of the glands, receives spiral arteries and is shed. The deeper basalis contains lower portions of the glands, receives straight arteries and remains to regenerate the functionalis.

questions.text: Name the three broadly arranged smooth muscle strata of the myometrium from inside out.
questions.explanation: Myometrial smooth muscle bundles interweave, making the boundaries between these strata indistinct.
questions.modelAnswer: The inner stratum submucosum lies next to the endometrium. The middle stratum vasculare contains many large vessels. The outer stratum subserosum lies toward the uterine surface. The layers are poorly demarcated.

questions.text: Why does contraction of the vessel-rich middle myometrium limit bleeding after placental separation?
questions.explanation: Vessel compression by contracted uterine muscle contributes to postpartum hemostasis.
questions.modelAnswer: Interlacing smooth muscle bundles contract around uterine vessels and compress their lumina, reducing blood flow from the placental site.

questions.text: How does rising estrogen affect myometrial smooth muscle during the ovarian cycle?
questions.explanation: The course links cyclic myocyte size to the changing estrogen environment.
questions.modelAnswer: Estrogen promotes growth of myometrial smooth muscle. The cells increase in size during the estrogen-dominant part of the cycle.

questions.text: List the principal components of menstrual discharge.
questions.explanation: The shedding tissue comes from the functionalis of the endometrium.
questions.modelAnswer: It contains blood, shed endometrial tissue including epithelial fragments, and mucus or other genital tract secretions.

questions.text: A boy with early virilization and elevated testosterone has a testosterone-secreting testicular tumor. Which normal cell type is the likely counterpart of the tumor cells?
questions.explanation: Leydig cells in the testicular interstitium synthesize testosterone. Sertoli cells support developing germ cells, and myoid cells are contractile.

questions.text: Which feature is expected in Leydig cells on electron microscopy?
questions.explanation: Lipid droplets provide precursors for steroid synthesis. Leydig cells also have abundant smooth ER and mitochondria with tubular cristae.

questions.text: Which change normally occurs as sperm pass through the epididymis?
questions.explanation: Epididymal maturation enables progressive motility. Meiosis and the formation of the acrosome and flagellum occur in the seminiferous epithelium.
options: Completion of the first meiotic division

questions.text: Which function is performed by Sertoli cells in adult seminiferous tubules?
questions.explanation: Sertoli cells provide structural and metabolic support within the seminiferous epithelium. Leydig cells secrete testosterone and peritubular myoid cells contract.

questions.text: Which cytoskeletal components help Sertoli cells reposition developing germ cells within the seminiferous epithelium?
questions.explanation: Sertoli-cell microtubules and actin filaments contribute to germ-cell positioning and movement.

questions.text: Which cellular feature is typical of the connective tissue stroma of the ovarian cortex?
questions.explanation: The ovarian cortical stroma contains spindle-shaped connective tissue cells and surrounds follicles in different stages.

questions.text: Which enzyme in ovarian granulosa cells converts androgen precursors from the theca interna into estrogens?
questions.explanation: Aromatase converts androgens into estrogens. The other enzymes catalyze different steroid conversions.

questions.text: How is the mucosa of the uterine tube lined?
questions.explanation: Simple columnar ciliated and nonciliated secretory cells line the uterine tube. The mucosa is especially folded in the ampulla.
options: Pseudostratified columnar with ciliated and principal cells
Simple cuboidal with brush-border and secretory cells
Simple columnar with ciliated and secretory cells
Stratified columnar with superficial mucus-secreting cells

questions.text: Which tissue forms the maternal part of the placenta?
questions.explanation: The decidua basalis is the modified endometrium beneath the implanted embryo. The chorion frondosum contributes the fetal part.

questions.text: Which arterial branches directly supply the basal layer of the endometrium?
questions.explanation: Straight arteries supply the basalis. Spiral arteries supply the functionalis, which is shed during menstruation.

questions.text: What is the cellular origin of the renin-secreting granular cells at the vascular pole of a renal corpuscle?
questions.explanation: The granular cells are modified smooth muscle cells, chiefly in the afferent arteriole. Macula densa and extraglomerular mesangial cells are separate parts of the same apparatus.

questions.text: Which nephron segment has a simple squamous epithelial lining?
questions.explanation: Thin limbs are lined by flattened cells. The proximal and distal convoluted tubules and thick ascending limb have cuboidal epithelium.
options: Thin limb of the loop of Henle
Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

questions.text: Which apical feature distinguishes distal convoluted tubular cells from proximal convoluted tubular cells?
questions.explanation: Distal convoluted tubular cells have few short apical microvilli. Proximal cells have a prominent brush border.

questions.text: Which structure allows umbrella cells to add membrane to their luminal surface as the bladder fills?
questions.explanation: Fusiform vesicles store uroplakin-rich membrane that can be added to the apical surface as umbrella cells flatten.

questions.text: Which organ has a highly branched, labyrinthine mucosa with secretory epithelium surrounded by a smooth muscle coat?
questions.explanation: The seminal vesicle has branching mucosal folds that give a labyrinthine appearance on section. The epididymis has a stereociliated duct and the ductus deferens has a prominent muscular wall.

questions.text: At the cervical transformation zone, which epithelial change normally occurs?
questions.explanation: Squamous metaplasia replaces exposed columnar epithelium at the transformation zone. The ectocervix normally has nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
options: Columnar epithelium is replaced by squamous epithelium
Columnar epithelium develops a ciliated pseudostratified lining

questions.text: Which structure expands distally to form the glans penis?
questions.explanation: The corpus spongiosum surrounds the penile urethra and expands to form the glans. The corpora cavernosa are paired dorsal erectile bodies.

questions.text: Which gland pattern is typical near the end of the proliferative phase of the endometrium?
questions.explanation: In the late proliferative phase glands are narrow and relatively straight. Secretory vacuoles and tortuous gland profiles develop after ovulation.

questions.text: What is the chromosome complement of a primary spermatocyte in prophase I?
questions.explanation: DNA replication has occurred before meiosis I. The cell is diploid and each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids.

questions.text: What is the main role of peritubular myoid cells around the seminiferous tubules?
questions.explanation: Peritubular myoid cells are contractile and help move luminal contents. Tight junctions between Sertoli cells form the blood–testis barrier.

questions.text: Which event defines the acrosome reaction during fertilization?
questions.explanation: The acrosome reaction releases stored enzymes that aid sperm passage through the oocyte's surrounding coat. Cortical granules are released from the oocyte in a separate reaction.
options: Assembly of acrosomal granules in a spermatid
Release of enzymes from the sperm acrosome
Release of cortical granules from the oocyte
Formation of the mitochondrial sheath in the sperm

questions.text: Which Sertoli-cell hormone provides negative feedback on pituitary FSH release?
questions.explanation: Inhibin B suppresses FSH release. Anti-Müllerian hormone acts on fetal Müllerian ducts, and androgen-binding protein retains testosterone in the tubular environment.

questions.text: Which description fits a secondary spermatocyte immediately after meiosis I?
questions.explanation: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes. Each secondary spermatocyte still has joined sister chromatids until meiosis II.
options: It has 23 chromosomes, each with two chromatids.
It has 46 chromosomes, each with two chromatids.
It has 23 chromosomes, each with one chromatid.
It has 46 chromosomes, each with one chromatid.

questions.text: Which cytoplasmic appearance fits a Leydig cell in routine testicular histology?
questions.explanation: Leydig cells have acidophilic cytoplasm with lipid droplets that can leave small clear spaces in routine sections.
options: Basophilic cytoplasm with conspicuous zymogen granules
Pale cytoplasm with apical mucin droplets
Basophilic cytoplasm with coarse secretory granules

questions.text: Which microscopic arrangement is typical of Leydig cells in the testis?
questions.explanation: Leydig cells form interstitial groups near blood vessels. Reinke crystalloids can be present but are not required to identify the cell population.
options: Tall cells at the base of seminiferous tubules
Cuboidal cells lining channels in the mediastinum

questions.text: Where does sperm capacitation normally take place after ejaculation?
questions.explanation: Capacitation involves changes that prepare sperm for fertilization after ejaculation. It precedes acrosomal exocytosis.
options: In the duct of the epididymis
In the lumen of the ductus deferens

questions.text: Which duct connects the seminiferous tubules directly to the rete testis?
questions.explanation: Tubuli recti are the straight segments between seminiferous tubules and rete testis. Efferent ductules leave the rete and lead toward the epididymis.

questions.text: Which structure is lined by principal cells with long, nonmotile stereocilia?
questions.explanation: The principal cells of the epididymal duct have stereocilia, which are elongated microvilli. Efferent ductules contain cells with motile cilia.

questions.text: Which description fits the secretion of the seminal vesicles?
questions.explanation: Seminal vesicles contribute viscous, yellowish, fructose-rich fluid to semen. Bulbourethral glands contribute lubricating mucus.
options: Thin milky fluid with proteolytic enzymes
Watery fluid with a high concentration of urea
Viscous yellowish fluid rich in fructose

questions.text: How are the secretory glands of the prostate classified?
questions.explanation: The prostate has branched ducts and secretory end pieces with tubular and alveolar features.

questions.text: Which description applies to the bulbourethral glands?
questions.explanation: The bulbourethral glands, also called Cowper glands, produce mucus released into the proximal spongy urethra.
options: Absorption of fluid from testicular ducts

questions.text: What forms the trabeculae between vascular spaces in penile erectile tissue?
questions.explanation: Erectile trabeculae contain smooth muscle and fibroelastic connective tissue. Their smooth muscle tone helps regulate filling of the vascular spaces.
options: Reticular fibers with cartilage and fat
Smooth muscle with collagen and elastin
Dense elastic fibers with skeletal muscle

questions.text: A patient has a varicocele. Which structure is abnormally dilated?
questions.explanation: A varicocele is dilation of the veins in the pampiniform plexus of the spermatic cord.
options: Superficial dorsal vein of the penis

questions.text: Sperm are present in seminiferous tubules on biopsy, but absent on repeated semen analysis. Which finding best explains sperm production with failure of transport?
questions.explanation: Bilateral absence of the ductus deferens prevents sperm from reaching the ejaculate despite preserved spermatogenesis.
options: Bilateral absence of the ductus deferens
Failure of Leydig cells to make testosterone

questions.text: Which combination of features identifies a proximal convoluted tubule in routine histology?
questions.explanation: Proximal tubules have a prominent brush border and indistinct lateral cell boundaries. Distal tubules have a clearer lumen and lack a prominent brush border.
options: Flat cells with nuclei projecting into a broad lumen
Cuboidal cells with a brush border and indistinct cell boundaries
Pale cuboidal cells with distinct boundaries and a clear lumen
Pseudostratified cells with long stereocilia and a scalloped lumen

questions.text: During which stage do nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes undergo crossing over in a primary spermatocyte?
questions.explanation: Homologs synapse during zygotene. Crossing over is classically assigned to pachytene of prophase I.

questions.text: Which structure forms a temporary microtubule sheath around the elongating spermatid nucleus?
questions.explanation: The manchette forms during spermatid elongation and contributes to nuclear shaping. The permanent tail structures have different locations and roles.

questions.text: Which cells are commonly seen in seminiferous tubule sections because they spend a prolonged time in prophase I?
questions.explanation: Primary spermatocytes spend a prolonged period in prophase I. Secondary spermatocytes enter meiosis II soon after forming and are seen less often.

questions.text: Which filament system forms the nine peripheral doublets and two central singlets of the sperm axoneme?
questions.explanation: The axoneme has a 9+2 arrangement of microtubules. Outer dense fibers and the mitochondrial sheath lie outside it.

questions.text: Which product is released mainly by Leydig cells rather than Sertoli cells?
questions.explanation: Leydig cells secrete testosterone. Sertoli cells produce androgen-binding protein and inhibin B and secrete anti-Müllerian hormone during fetal development.

questions.text: Which named cytoplasmic inclusions can occur in Leydig cells?
questions.explanation: Reinke crystalloids may occur in the cytoplasm of interstitial Leydig cells.

questions.text: Into which part of the urethra do the bulbourethral ducts open?
questions.explanation: The ducts of the bulbourethral glands pass into the bulb of the penis and open into the proximal spongy urethra.

questions.text: Which layers lie outside the basal lamina of an antral ovarian follicle?
questions.explanation: The theca interna and externa develop from surrounding ovarian stroma and lie outside the follicle's basal lamina. Granulosa cells lie inside it.

questions.text: Which function is supported by the usual direction of ciliary beating in the uterine tube?
questions.explanation: Tubal cilia beat predominantly toward the uterus and help move the oocyte or early embryo. Tubal smooth muscle also contributes to transport.
options: Movement of sperm from the uterus into the peritoneum
Movement of an ovulated oocyte farther from the uterus
Transport of tubal contents toward the uterus
Transport of tubal secretions out through the fimbriae

questions.text: Which vessels supply the endometrial layer shed at menstruation?
questions.explanation: Spiral arteries supply the functionalis, which is shed. Straight arteries supply the deeper basalis.

questions.text: Which event conventionally marks day 1 of the menstrual cycle?
questions.explanation: Day 1 is the first day of menstrual bleeding. Ovulation and the secretory phase follow later in the same cycle.
options: Peak of the midcycle LH surge

questions.text: What is the predominant tissue in the wall of the uterine cervix?
questions.explanation: The cervical wall is predominantly collagenous with elastic fibers and comparatively little smooth muscle. The uterine body has a much thicker smooth muscle coat.

questions.text: Which finding is expected in normal vaginal mucosa?
questions.explanation: Healthy vaginal mucosa has a glycogen-rich, nonkeratinized stratified squamous lining and lacks intrinsic mucous glands.
options: Mucous glands opening through the epithelium
Simple columnar cells with motile cilia
Fully keratinized cells in a cornified surface

questions.text: Which glomerular cells phagocytose debris that accumulates near the capillary basement membrane?
questions.explanation: Intraglomerular mesangial cells support the capillary tuft and remove debris by phagocytosis. Extraglomerular mesangial cells lie at the vascular pole.

questions.text: Which change prolongs cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation after nitric oxide signaling?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide increases cyclic GMP in smooth muscle. PDE5 inhibition slows cyclic GMP breakdown and prolongs smooth muscle relaxation.

questions.text: Which placental hormone stimulates fetal Leydig cells to produce testosterone early in development?
questions.explanation: Human chorionic gonadotropin activates the LH receptor on fetal Leydig cells and stimulates testosterone production.

questions.text: Which change allows copious milk secretion to begin after placental delivery?
questions.explanation: High placental estrogen and progesterone limit the milk-producing action of prolactin during pregnancy. Their fall after placental delivery permits copious milk secretion.
options: Reduced prolactin release from the anterior pituitary
Continued rise in placental estrogen and progesterone
Withdrawal of placental estrogen and progesterone
Suppression of oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary

questions.text: During suckling, which response causes milk ejection from mammary alveoli?
questions.explanation: Oxytocin released from the posterior pituitary contracts myoepithelial cells and ejects milk. Prolactin supports milk synthesis.
options: Prolactin stimulates the synthesis of milk proteins
Dopamine suppresses anterior pituitary prolactin release
Vasopressin increases water absorption by collecting ducts

questions.text: Which role does prostate-specific antigen normally play in semen after ejaculation?
questions.explanation: PSA is a prostatic protease that breaks down proteins in the seminal coagulum, helping semen liquefy after ejaculation.
options: Supplying fructose as a substrate for sperm
Triggering membrane fusion at the oocyte
Maintaining the sperm head's acrosomal cap

questions.text: Which endocrine change helps explain delayed return of ovulation during frequent breastfeeding?
questions.explanation: Suckling reduces hypothalamic GnRH pulse activity. This lowers gonadotropin support for follicle maturation and ovulation.
options: Enhanced ovarian estradiol feedback at midcycle

questions.text: Which description fits capillary endothelium in a normal adult glomerular tuft?
questions.explanation: Adult glomerular capillaries have abundant endothelial fenestrae that typically lack diaphragms. The basement membrane and podocyte slit diaphragms are separate components of the barrier.

questions.text: Which feature can be seen in the superficial umbrella cells of bladder urothelium?
questions.explanation: Umbrella cells may be binucleated. They cover the luminal surface and flatten as the bladder distends.
options: An apical brush border for absorption
Motile cilia on the luminal surface
Keratinization over most of the luminal surface

questions.text: Which proteins form the thickened plaques on the luminal membrane of bladder umbrella cells?
questions.explanation: Uroplakins assemble into apical plaques. The plaques and tight junctions contribute to the urothelial barrier.

questions.text: Where is the macula densa located in relation to its own renal corpuscle?
questions.explanation: The macula densa is a specialized patch at the junction of the thick ascending limb and distal convoluted tubule. It lies beside the arterioles at the vascular pole.
options: In the proximal tubule at the urinary pole
In the distal tubular segment at the vascular pole
In the cortical collecting duct at the vascular pole
In the thin descending limb near the papilla

questions.text: Which collecting-duct cell type secretes hydrogen ions into the lumen during an acid load?
questions.explanation: Type A intercalated cells secrete hydrogen ions. Type B intercalated cells secrete bicarbonate, while principal cells regulate water and sodium handling.

questions.text: Which structure produces the basal striated appearance of proximal tubular epithelial cells?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria lie between basal membrane infoldings, producing basal striations and supporting active transport.
options: Apical microvilli with an underlying terminal web
Stacks of rough ER surrounding the nucleus
Tight junctions along the apical lateral membrane

questions.text: Which gland contributes a fructose-rich secretion to semen?
questions.explanation: Seminal vesicles supply fructose, a substrate that sperm can use for energy. Bulbourethral and urethral glands contribute mucus.

questions.text: What is the normal order of germ-cell development within the seminiferous tubules?
questions.explanation: Spermatogonia give rise to spermatocytes. Meiosis produces spermatids, which differentiate into spermatozoa.

questions.text: Which junctions physically separate basal and adluminal compartments within seminiferous tubules?
questions.explanation: Tight junctions between Sertoli cells partition the seminiferous epithelium. The barrier is epithelial and lies close to the basal compartment.
options: Gap junctions between neighboring germ cells
Tight junctions between vascular endothelial cells
Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells
Adherens junctions between peritubular myoid cells

questions.text: Which cells are fetal macrophages in the stroma of chorionic villi?
questions.explanation: Hofbauer cells are macrophages in villous connective tissue. Trophoblast forms the epithelial covering of the villus, and decidual cells are maternal.

questions.text: Which testicular covering thickens posteriorly to form the mediastinum testis?
questions.explanation: The mediastinum is a posterior thickening of the fibrous tunica albuginea. The rete testis lies within it.

questions.text: Which change occurs during the acrosomal phase of spermiogenesis in the course description?
questions.explanation: During the acrosomal phase the nucleus condenses further, elongates, and flattens. Mitochondrial sheath formation and residual cytoplasm removal occur later.
options: Mitochondria pass beyond the annulus into the principal piece
The spermatid nucleus elongates and becomes flatter
Sister chromatids separate at the second meiotic division
Residual cytoplasm is expelled and removed by Sertoli cells

questions.text: Which cell is the first haploid stage of spermatogenesis, and what is the state of its chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Haploid refers to one set of homologs. DNA content remains doubled within each chromosome until sister chromatids separate.
questions.modelAnswer: The secondary spermatocyte is the first haploid stage. It forms after meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes. It has 23 chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids, until meiosis II separates them.

questions.text: What is the principal role of androgen-binding protein released into seminiferous tubules?
questions.explanation: Sertoli cells produce androgen-binding protein. It binds testosterone and helps maintain a high androgen concentration in the tubular environment.
options: Stimulating pituitary secretion of luteinizing hormone
Converting testosterone to estradiol in the interstitium
Maintaining a high local concentration of testosterone
Activating Leydig-cell androgen receptors at the vascular pole

questions.text: Which epithelial lining is expected in the ductus deferens?
questions.explanation: The ductus deferens has a pseudostratified columnar lining with stereocilia. Its prominent three-layer smooth muscle coat propels sperm during emission.
options: Simple squamous epithelium with delicate basal lamina
Stratified squamous epithelium with keratinized surface
Simple columnar epithelium with motile cilia

questions.text: Which finding defines cryptorchidism?
questions.explanation: Cryptorchidism means incomplete testicular descent. A testis may remain at different points along its normal descent path.
options: A testis has failed to descend into the scrotum.
A testis fails to develop from its gonadal primordium.
Fluid accumulates between layers of the tunica vaginalis.
The pampiniform veins become dilated and tortuous.

questions.text: How can a varicocele impair sperm production even when androgen secretion is preserved?
questions.explanation: The pampiniform plexus normally exchanges heat with arterial blood entering the testis. Disturbed venous drainage can impair cooling and raise testicular temperature.
options: By blocking fructose secretion from seminal vesicles
By reducing countercurrent cooling of testicular blood
By preventing contraction of the ductus deferens wall
By stopping removal of residual bodies from spermatids

questions.text: Which event helps restore venous drainage from the corpora cavernosa during normal detumescence?
questions.explanation: As cavernosal smooth muscle tone returns, sinusoidal filling falls and the compression of venous outflow eases.
options: Further relaxation of cavernosal smooth muscle
Return of cavernosal smooth muscle tone
A sustained increase in cyclic GMP signaling

questions.text: Describe how podocytes contribute to the glomerular filtration barrier.
questions.explanation: Podocytes are the visceral epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule and provide the outer cellular layer of the filtration barrier.
questions.modelAnswer: Podocyte foot processes wrap around the outside of glomerular capillaries and interdigitate. Slit diaphragms bridge gaps between adjacent foot processes. Podocytes also contribute to the formation and maintenance of the glomerular basement membrane.

questions.text: Describe the glomerular basement membrane and explain its role in filtration.
questions.explanation: The basement membrane works together with the endothelial surface and podocyte slit diaphragms to restrict passage of plasma proteins.
questions.modelAnswer: The glomerular basement membrane is a shared extracellular matrix between capillary endothelium and podocytes. Its type IV collagen network provides structural support, and the organized matrix contributes to limiting passage of larger macromolecules as part of the whole glomerular filtration barrier.

questions.text: List the three groups of renal collecting tubules described in the histology chapter.
questions.explanation: Papillary ducts empty at the renal papilla. Connecting tubules bring fluid from distal convoluted tubules to the collecting system.
questions.modelAnswer: Cortical collecting tubules, medullary collecting tubules, and papillary ducts, also called ducts of Bellini.

questions.text: Which two structural features of umbrella cells help the urothelium form a barrier against urine?
questions.explanation: The plaques and junctions protect underlying tissue through complementary transcellular and paracellular barriers.
questions.modelAnswer: The apical surface contains thick uroplakin-rich membrane plaques that limit passage across the cells. Tight junctions between neighboring umbrella cells restrict passage between them.

questions.text: Describe the main supportive, barrier, phagocytic and secretory functions of Sertoli cells.
questions.explanation: Sertoli cells maintain the environment for spermatogenesis and have distinct fetal and postpubertal secretory roles.
questions.modelAnswer: Sertoli cells support and nourish developing germ cells. Basolateral tight junctions form the blood–testis barrier. Sertoli cells phagocytose residual cytoplasm. They produce tubular fluid and androgen-binding protein, participate in local steroid metabolism, and secrete inhibin B and, during fetal development, anti-Müllerian hormone.

questions.text: Which region of the epididymis contains the efferent ductules, and which structures do the ductules connect?
questions.explanation: The efferent ductules converge on the epididymal duct, which continues through the body and tail.
questions.modelAnswer: The efferent ductules contribute to the head of the epididymis. They carry sperm from the rete testis into the epididymal duct.

questions.text: Summarize the proliferation, growth, and meiotic maturation stages of oogenesis.
questions.explanation: The two meiotic divisions resume at different times. Ovulation follows completion of meiosis I.
questions.modelAnswer: Oogonia multiply mitotically in fetal life. They grow into primary oocytes, enter meiosis I, and arrest in prophase I. Before ovulation a selected primary oocyte completes meiosis I, producing the secondary oocyte and first polar body. The secondary oocyte arrests in metaphase II and normally completes meiosis II after fertilization.

questions.text: Which structure separates granulosa cells from vascular ovarian stroma in a growing follicle?
questions.explanation: Nutrients can reach granulosa and the oocyte without blood vessels entering the granulosa layer.
questions.modelAnswer: The follicular basal lamina separates the granulosa layer from the surrounding stroma and thecal vessels. This keeps blood vessels outside the granulosa compartment of the intact follicle.

questions.text: Describe the follicular cell layers surrounding the oocyte in a multilaminar primary follicle.
questions.explanation: Granulosa proliferation changes the lining from a single layer to a multilayered epithelium.
questions.modelAnswer: Several layers of granulosa cells surround the oocyte and its zona pellucida. The innermost radially arranged granulosa cells adjacent to the zona pellucida form the corona radiata in the course description.

questions.text: What is the ovarian stigma and what happens at that site during ovulation?
questions.explanation: The stigma develops where the mature follicle bulges against the ovarian surface.
questions.modelAnswer: The stigma is the pale, thinned area of the ovarian surface over the preovulatory follicle. The follicle ruptures at this weakened site and releases the oocyte with surrounding cells.

questions.text: In the course description of follicular-wall remodeling, which enzymes are associated with degradation of the basal lamina and collagen in the tunica albuginea?
questions.explanation: Proteolysis weakens the follicle wall and the ovarian surface at the future rupture site.
questions.modelAnswer: Plasmin is associated with basal-lamina degradation. Collagenases degrade collagen in the tunica albuginea.

questions.text: Describe the structural events in the dominant follicle after the LH surge that allow ovulation.
questions.explanation: Oocyte maturation, cumulus expansion, and local wall weakening coordinate release after the LH surge.
questions.modelAnswer: Meiosis I yields the secondary oocyte and first polar body. Hyaluronan contributes to expansion of the cumulus around the oocyte. Proteolysis and tissue remodeling weaken the follicle wall at the stigma. The follicle ruptures, releasing the oocyte with its surrounding cumulus cells.

questions.text: List the segments of the uterine tube from the ovarian end toward the uterine cavity.
questions.explanation: The fimbriae are projections from the infundibulum. The intramural segment passes through the uterine wall.
questions.modelAnswer: The infundibulum bears the fimbriae, followed by the ampulla, isthmus, and intramural segment.

questions.text: At a thin exchange site in a term placental villus, what separates maternal blood from fetal blood, and what does this barrier do?
questions.explanation: At term fetal capillaries approach the trophoblast at specialized thin exchange sites, shortening diffusion distance.
questions.modelAnswer: Maternal blood contacts syncytiotrophoblast. At a thin exchange site, closely apposed trophoblastic and fetal-capillary basement membranes separate it from the underlying fetal capillary endothelium. Cytotrophoblast is sparse and villous stroma is greatly reduced locally. The barrier permits exchange of gases, nutrients, and wastes while maintaining separate maternal and fetal circulations.

questions.text: In which organ do corpora amylacea commonly accumulate in glandular lumina with age?
questions.explanation: Corpora amylacea are rounded concretions within the lumina of prostatic glands. They may enlarge or calcify with age.

questions.text: Which mitotically active germ cells reside along the basal lamina of the seminiferous epithelium?
questions.explanation: Spermatogonia lie in the basal compartment and can proliferate by mitosis. Spermatids and secondary spermatocytes are later stages.

questions.text: Which cells form the visceral epithelium of Bowman's capsule?
questions.explanation: Podocytes are modified visceral epithelial cells. Their foot processes contact the outer aspect of the shared basement membrane.

questions.text: Compare the epithelial cells of the parietal and visceral layers of Bowman's capsule.
questions.explanation: The parietal layer outlines Bowman's space, while the visceral layer contributes to the filtration barrier.
questions.modelAnswer: The parietal layer is simple squamous epithelium. The visceral layer is formed by podocytes, which are modified epithelial cells with processes that cover glomerular capillaries.

questions.text: Relate the brush border, basal striations, and indistinct cell borders of proximal convoluted tubules to their ultrastructure.
questions.explanation: These structures increase membrane area and support active solute transport.
questions.modelAnswer: The brush border consists of tightly packed apical microvilli. Basal striations reflect plasma membrane infoldings with elongated mitochondria. Indistinct lateral cell borders reflect extensive interdigitations between neighboring cells.

questions.text: Name the three cellular components of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.
questions.explanation: The apparatus lies at the vascular pole of the renal corpuscle. Granular cells release renin.
questions.modelAnswer: Macula densa cells of the distal tubular segment, granular juxtaglomerular cells derived from arteriolar smooth muscle, and extraglomerular mesangial or Lacis cells.

questions.text: Compare the proximal and distal female urethral lining with the usual penile urethral lining and the fossa navicularis in the course description.
questions.explanation: The lining varies by segment, so proximal and distal landmarks matter when identifying the epithelium.
questions.modelAnswer: The female urethra has urothelium proximally and nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium distally. Most of the penile urethra has a columnar lining, described as stratified columnar in the course. It changes to nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium at the fossa navicularis.

questions.text: Which divisions make up the maturation phase of spermatocytogenesis, and what cells and chromosome complements result?
questions.explanation: There is no intervening DNA replication between meiosis I and meiosis II.
questions.modelAnswer: A replicated primary spermatocyte divides by meiosis I into two secondary spermatocytes. Each has 23 chromosomes with two sister chromatids per chromosome. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, yielding four spermatids in total. Each has 23 chromosomes with one chromatid per chromosome.

questions.text: What forms the blood–testis barrier, which compartments does it separate, and what does this separation accomplish?
questions.explanation: Primary spermatocytes move through the barrier as junctions remodel.
questions.modelAnswer: Basolateral tight junctions between neighboring Sertoli cells divide the seminiferous epithelium into basal and adluminal compartments. Spermatogonia occupy the basal compartment. Later germ cells develop in the regulated adluminal environment, which limits their exposure to circulating immune factors.

questions.text: Compare the lining of the epididymal duct with the lining of the ejaculatory duct in the course histology table.
questions.explanation: Stereocilia are nonmotile microvilli. The ducts have distinct locations and functions along the outflow tract.
questions.modelAnswer: The epididymal duct has pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereociliated principal cells and basal cells. The ejaculatory duct is described as having simple columnar epithelium.

questions.text: What makes up one renal lobe?
questions.explanation: A renal lobe is organized around a medullary pyramid. The associated cortex includes cortical tissue overlying and closely related to the pyramid.
options: One medullary ray and its surrounding cortical labyrinth
Two neighboring pyramids without intervening tissue
A cortical column separating two medullary pyramids
One medullary pyramid and its associated cortex

questions.text: What structures make up a renal cortical lobule?
questions.explanation: A lobule is organized around a medullary ray within the cortex. A medullary pyramid and associated cortex form a renal lobe.
options: A medullary ray and the nearby cortical labyrinth
One medullary pyramid and the cortex overlying its base
A renal papilla and the minor calyx that surrounds it
A cortical column between adjacent medullary pyramids

questions.text: Which structure opens at the renal papilla rather than lying in the renal cortex?
questions.explanation: Papillary ducts are terminal collecting ducts that open at the papillary tip into a minor calyx. The other structures are cortical.

questions.text: What is a renal column of Bertin?
questions.explanation: Renal columns are extensions of cortex between adjacent medullary pyramids. A cortical lobule is organized around a medullary ray.
options: Cortical tissue surrounding a medullary ray
Medullary tissue extending to a minor calyx
Medullary tissue forming a renal papilla

questions.text: Which structures form a medullary ray within the renal cortex?
questions.explanation: Medullary rays are cortical bundles of straight nephron segments and cortical collecting ducts. Convoluted tubules and renal corpuscles occupy the surrounding cortical labyrinth.
options: Renal corpuscles and proximal convoluted tubules
Distal convoluted tubules and cortical capillaries
Straight nephron segments and collecting ducts
Papillary ducts and the walls of adjacent minor calyces

questions.text: Which combination of tubular structures is found within a renal medullary pyramid?
questions.explanation: Pyramids contain medullary portions of loops of Henle, collecting ducts, and their accompanying vessels. Renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules are cortical.
options: Renal corpuscles and proximal convoluted tubules
Distal convoluted tubules and Bowman's capsules
Glomerular tufts and cortical collecting tubules
Loops of Henle and medullary collecting ducts

questions.text: Which cortical region contains renal corpuscles and neighboring convoluted tubules?
questions.explanation: The cortical labyrinth contains renal corpuscles and proximal and distal convoluted tubules. A medullary ray contains straight segments and collecting ducts.

questions.text: Which structure belongs to the collecting system rather than to a nephron proper?
questions.explanation: A nephron consists of a renal corpuscle and its tubule. Papillary ducts receive urine from the collecting system downstream of multiple nephrons.
options: Thick limb of the loop of Henle
Bowman's capsule with its capillary tuft

questions.text: Which arrangement describes Bowman's capsule around the glomerular tuft?
questions.explanation: Visceral podocytes cover the glomerular capillaries. Parietal squamous epithelium forms the outer boundary of Bowman’s urinary space.
options: A single squamous layer directly covers capillary endothelium
Two endothelial layers enclose Bowman’s urinary space
Visceral and parietal layers bound the urinary space
Two layers of cuboidal tubular cells enclose the tuft

questions.text: Which structure lies next to the vascular pole but belongs to a tubule outside the renal corpuscle?
questions.explanation: The macula densa is part of the distal tubular segment near the vascular pole. It senses tubular fluid, while the nearby corpuscle filters plasma.

questions.text: Where are the renal corpuscles of juxtamedullary nephrons located?
questions.explanation: Juxtamedullary corpuscles lie in deep cortex near the corticomedullary boundary. Their long loops extend into the medulla.
options: In the interstitial space of the renal sinus

questions.text: Which epithelial type lines the parietal layer of Bowman's capsule away from the urinary pole?
questions.explanation: The parietal layer is a thin simple squamous lining on a basal lamina. It becomes continuous with cuboidal proximal tubular epithelium at the urinary pole.

questions.text: Which structure directly receives filtrate from Bowman's space at the urinary pole?
questions.explanation: At the urinary pole, Bowman’s space continues into the proximal tubule. Afferent and efferent arterioles enter or leave at the vascular pole.

questions.text: Which cell type supports glomerular capillary loops without forming one of the three direct filtration layers?
questions.explanation: The direct filtration barrier consists of fenestrated endothelium, the shared basement membrane, and podocyte slit diaphragms. Mesangial cells support the tuft between capillary loops.
options: Podocytes attached to the basement membrane
Parietal epithelial cells lining Bowman's capsule

questions.text: Which mediator can promote contraction of intraglomerular mesangial cells?
questions.explanation: Mesangial cells respond to angiotensin II. Their contraction changes the surface area of glomerular capillaries available for filtration.
options: Antidiuretic hormone acting on collecting ducts

questions.text: Which pericyte-like cells lie between the capillary loops within the glomerular tuft?
questions.explanation: Intraglomerular mesangial cells occupy the mesangium within the tuft. Lacis cells are outside the tuft at the vascular pole.

questions.text: Which structures flank the slits bridged by slit diaphragms in the glomerular filtration barrier?
questions.explanation: Interdigitating podocyte foot processes are separated by filtration slits. Slit diaphragms span the gaps.

questions.text: What accounts for the basal striations of distal convoluted tubular cells?
questions.explanation: Basal infoldings increase membrane surface area and are associated with mitochondria. These features support active transport in the distal tubule.
options: Long microvilli projecting into the lumen
Glycogen and secretory granules near the basal pole
Dense lysosomes arranged along the basal surface

questions.text: Which nephron population typically has the longest loops extending into the deepest medulla?
questions.explanation: Juxtamedullary nephrons have corpuscles near the corticomedullary boundary and relatively long loops that extend deeper into the medulla.
options: Nephrons next to the renal capsule

questions.text: Which U-shaped nephron segment connects the proximal and distal parts of the tubule?
questions.explanation: The loop of Henle descends toward the medulla and returns toward the cortex. Its descending and ascending limbs are distinct from the collecting system.

questions.text: Which combination of features favors distal rather than proximal convoluted tubule on routine histology?
questions.explanation: Distal tubules have sparse apical microvilli and a clearer lumen. Proximal cells have a prominent brush border and less distinct lateral outlines.
options: Tall cuboidal cells and a thick apical brush border
Poorly defined cell borders and a fuzzy lumen
A clear lumen and short sparse microvilli
A stratified lining with taller apical cells

questions.text: What does aldosterone promote in principal cells of the cortical collecting duct?
questions.explanation: Aldosterone increases apical sodium channel activity and basolateral sodium–potassium pump activity in principal cells. Sodium reabsorption helps drive potassium secretion.
options: A reduction in apical sodium entry and potassium secretion
An increase in luminal chloride uptake with no effect on sodium
An increase in hydrogen ion uptake paired with potassium retention
An increase in sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion

questions.text: Which cells release renin at the vascular pole of a renal corpuscle?
questions.explanation: Granular juxtaglomerular cells are modified arteriolar smooth muscle cells. The macula densa influences their release of renin.

questions.text: What feature of tubular fluid does the macula densa monitor for tubuloglomerular feedback?
questions.explanation: The macula densa senses luminal sodium chloride and signals to the afferent arteriole and renin-secreting granular cells.
options: Filtered albumin entering the urinary space
Glucose concentration in the collecting duct
Plasma renin arriving from the renal artery

questions.text: Where is the juxtaglomerular apparatus in relation to a renal corpuscle?
questions.explanation: The apparatus sits at the vascular pole, where the distal tubular segment approaches the afferent and efferent arterioles. The urinary pole leads into the proximal tubule.
options: At the urinary pole beside the proximal tubule
Inside Bowman’s space facing the capillary tuft
At the vascular pole beside the arterioles
At the tip of the papilla beside collecting ducts

questions.text: Which combination of epithelial cells lines the cortical collecting duct?
questions.explanation: Cortical collecting ducts contain principal cells for water and electrolyte handling and intercalated cells for acid–base regulation.
options: Macula densa and granular juxtaglomerular cells
Proximal tubular cells with prominent brush borders

questions.text: What epithelium lines the large papillary ducts near the area cribrosa in the course description?
questions.explanation: Papillary ducts are lined by tall columnar collecting-duct cells. Urothelium begins in the minor calyx downstream.

questions.text: Which renal region is supplied by the vasa recta?
questions.explanation: Vasa recta are straight vessels that carry blood into and out of the renal medulla, near loops of Henle and collecting ducts.
options: Outer cortex near the fibrous capsule
Medulla around the loops and collecting ducts
Renal pelvis and the proximal ureter

questions.text: Which second capillary bed normally receives blood from efferent arterioles of superficial cortical nephrons?
questions.explanation: Efferent arterioles from superficial glomeruli supply cortical peritubular capillaries. Efferent arterioles from juxtamedullary nephrons supply the medullary vasa recta.
options: Glomerular capillaries of an adjacent nephron
Medullary vessels accompanying long nephron loops
Stellate veins immediately beneath the renal capsule

questions.text: Which sequence traces arterial flow through the kidney immediately before blood reaches a glomerulus?
questions.explanation: Interlobar arteries ascend between pyramids. They give rise to arcuate arteries, which send cortical radiate branches into the cortex. Afferent arterioles branch from those vessels.

questions.text: Which arteries directly give rise to most afferent arterioles in the renal cortex?
questions.explanation: Cortical radiate, or interlobular, arteries give rise to the afferent arterioles that enter glomeruli. Arcuate and interlobar arteries are upstream.

questions.text: Which epithelium lines the ureteral lumen?
questions.explanation: The ureter has urothelium, with umbrella cells facing the lumen. Its smooth muscle moves urine toward the bladder by peristalsis.

questions.text: At the renal papilla, where does urine first enter a urothelium-lined collecting space?
questions.explanation: Papillary ducts contain tall collecting-duct epithelium and empty into a minor calyx, which is lined by urothelium.

questions.text: Which smooth muscle layer is added in the distal ureter to the inner longitudinal and circular layers?
questions.explanation: The distal ureter has inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal smooth muscle layers in the course description.

questions.text: Which arrangement does the course describe for detrusor smooth muscle as it approaches the bladder neck?
questions.explanation: Near the neck, the course describes inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal smooth muscle. Elsewhere much of the detrusor is interwoven.
options: Inner circular, middle longitudinal, outer longitudinal
Inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal
Inner longitudinal, middle longitudinal, outer circular
Inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer circular

questions.text: Which epithelium lines the prostatic urethra near its junction with the bladder in the course description?
questions.explanation: Urothelium continues from the bladder into the proximal prostatic urethra. The lining of nearby prostatic secretory glands is a separate structure.

questions.text: Which epithelium lines the fossa navicularis in the distal spongy urethra?
questions.explanation: The urethral lining becomes nonkeratinized stratified squamous at the fossa navicularis. It differs from the keratinized covering of the external skin.
options: Transitional epithelium with superficial umbrella cells

questions.text: Where do the short ducts of the urethral glands of Littre open?
questions.explanation: The glands of Littre contribute mucus to the penile or spongy urethral lumen. The prostatic ducts open separately into the prostatic urethra.

questions.text: Which pairing describes the female urethral lining near the bladder and at its distal end?
questions.explanation: The course describes transitional epithelium near the bladder and nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium distally.
options: Proximal stratified squamous and distal urothelium
Proximal urothelium and distal nonkeratinized stratified squamous
Proximal simple cuboidal and distal pseudostratified stereociliated
Proximal stratified columnar and distal keratinized stratified squamous

questions.text: How does the fenestrated endothelium of glomerular capillaries contribute to filtration?
questions.explanation: The endothelial layer is the first cellular component of the glomerular filtration barrier.
questions.modelAnswer: The fenestrae allow water and small dissolved solutes to leave the capillary, while the endothelial layer retains blood cells and platelets. The capillary endothelium acts together with the glomerular basement membrane and podocyte slit diaphragms.

questions.text: Describe the location and major functions of intraglomerular mesangial cells.
questions.explanation: Mesangial cells support the capillary tuft from between the loops.
questions.modelAnswer: These stellate cells lie between glomerular capillary loops. They provide structural support and produce mesangial matrix. They can contract, altering the available capillary surface, and clear trapped material by endocytosis or phagocytosis.

questions.text: Describe the seminiferous tubule wall, its two main epithelial cell populations, and their roles.
questions.explanation: The wall combines a producing epithelium with contractile cells outside it.
questions.modelAnswer: A basal lamina supports the seminiferous epithelium. Peritubular myoid cells surround the tubule and contract to help move luminal contents. Spermatogenic cells form successive stages of the germ-cell lineage. Sertoli cells extend from the basal lamina toward the lumen, support germ cells, and form tight junctions that partition the epithelium.

questions.text: Compare spermatogonia, primary and secondary spermatocytes, and spermatids by their position or appearance and next developmental step.
questions.explanation: The population next to the basal lamina differs from cells moving through meiosis and maturing toward the lumen.
questions.modelAnswer: Basal spermatogonia proliferate by mitosis and give rise to primary spermatocytes. Primary spermatocytes are relatively large and undergo meiosis I. Smaller, short-lived secondary spermatocytes undergo meiosis II. Small adluminal spermatids remodel into spermatozoa without further division.

questions.text: Outline the three main transitions of spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules.
questions.explanation: Incomplete cytokinesis leaves developing germ cells linked by cytoplasmic bridges during much of development.
questions.modelAnswer: Spermatogonia proliferate by mitosis and differentiate into primary spermatocytes. Meiosis I yields secondary spermatocytes and meiosis II yields haploid spermatids. Spermiogenesis remodels spermatids into spermatozoa without further cell division.

questions.text: Describe the origin, chromosomal complement, and next division of a primary spermatocyte after premeiotic DNA replication.
questions.explanation: The prolonged prophase helps make primary spermatocytes prominent in sections of seminiferous tubules.
questions.modelAnswer: It develops from the type B spermatogonial lineage. After DNA replication it has 46 chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids. It enters meiosis I, including a prolonged prophase in which homologous chromosomes pair and exchange segments. Meiosis I yields two secondary spermatocytes.

questions.text: How can primary spermatocytes, secondary spermatocytes, and spermatids be distinguished among the adluminal germ cells?
questions.explanation: The adluminal populations differ in size, nuclear appearance, and how long each stage lasts.
questions.modelAnswer: Primary spermatocytes are large and have prominent coarse chromatin during prophase I. Secondary spermatocytes are smaller and seldom seen because they pass quickly into meiosis II. Spermatids are small haploid cells near the lumen. Early spermatids are round, while late spermatids elongate and condense their nuclei.

questions.text: Outline the Golgi, cap, acrosomal and maturation phases of spermiogenesis.
questions.explanation: This remodeling converts a round haploid spermatid into a spermatozoon without another cell division.
questions.modelAnswer: In the Golgi phase, vesicles form and fuse into the acrosomal vesicle. In the cap phase it spreads over the anterior nucleus. During the acrosomal phase the nucleus elongates and condenses as the flagellum develops and mitochondria organize around the middle piece. During maturation, residual cytoplasm is shed and phagocytosed by Sertoli cells.

questions.text: Describe the major regions of a spermatozoon and explain how temperature and gonadotropins support spermatogenesis.
questions.explanation: Each sperm region has a specialized structure. The seminiferous environment depends on local temperature regulation and endocrine support.
questions.modelAnswer: The head contains a compact haploid nucleus and the acrosome. A connecting piece links the head to the flagellum. The middle piece has a mitochondrial sheath, the principal piece contains a fibrous sheath, and the end piece consists mainly of the axoneme and membrane. Spermatogenesis is supported by lower scrotal temperature, testosterone from LH-stimulated Leydig cells, and FSH action on Sertoli cells.

questions.text: Describe where Leydig cells are found and how their microscopic features support testosterone production.
questions.explanation: The interstitial location and steroidogenic organelles distinguish Leydig cells from the Sertoli cells within the tubule.
questions.modelAnswer: Leydig cells occur in clusters in the interstitial connective tissue between seminiferous tubules, near capillaries. They are polygonal cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm. Abundant smooth endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria with tubular cristae support steroid synthesis, and lipid droplets can supply cholesterol. LH stimulates testosterone production.

questions.text: Compare the duct of the epididymis and the ductus deferens by epithelial lining, lumen, muscle, and function.
questions.explanation: Epididymal maturation occurs before ejaculation. Capacitation usually occurs after ejaculation in the female reproductive tract.
questions.modelAnswer: Both ducts have pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia. The highly coiled epididymal duct has a comparatively broad lumen and a smooth muscle coat that thickens toward its tail. It supports sperm maturation and storage. The ductus deferens has a narrow, folded lumen and a thick smooth muscle coat with inner and outer longitudinal layers around a middle circular layer. It propels sperm during emission.

questions.text: Describe the histological structure of a mature Graafian follicle from the oocyte outward.
questions.explanation: The basal lamina separates avascular granulosa from the vascular steroidogenic theca interna.
questions.modelAnswer: The oocyte is surrounded by the zona pellucida and corona radiata. It is held on the cumulus oophorus, which projects into the large fluid-filled antrum. Mural granulosa cells line the antrum, and a basal lamina separates them from the theca. The vascular theca interna produces androgens used by granulosa cells for estrogen synthesis. The theca externa contains supporting fibrous tissue and smooth muscle cells.

questions.text: Explain how the corpus luteum forms, identify its two major lutein cell populations, and describe its fate with and without pregnancy.
questions.explanation: The corpus luteum is a transient endocrine structure derived from both granulosa and theca interna.
questions.modelAnswer: After ovulation, the ruptured follicle collapses and vascular tissue invades. Granulosa cells become large, relatively pale granulosa lutein cells, which secrete mainly progesterone. Theca interna cells become smaller, darker theca lutein cells, concentrated toward the periphery and in folds. Without pregnancy the corpus luteum regresses and leaves a fibrous corpus albicans. In early pregnancy, trophoblastic hCG maintains luteal steroid secretion until the placenta takes over.

questions.text: Describe the mucosa, muscularis, and serosa of the ampulla of the uterine tube.
questions.explanation: The ampulla has an especially elaborate folded mucosa and is the usual site of fertilization.
questions.modelAnswer: The mucosa has numerous branching folds of loose connective tissue lined by simple columnar epithelium with ciliated and nonciliated secretory cells.
