Cilia and smooth muscle activity contribute to transport, and secretory cells support the luminal environment. The muscularis has predominantly inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle. The serosa consists of connective tissue covered by mesothelium.

questions.text: Describe the glandular, stromal, and vascular changes in the endometrium during the secretory phase.
questions.explanation: The glandular and stromal changes evolve over the secretory phase as the endometrium becomes receptive to implantation.
questions.modelAnswer: After ovulation, progesterone acts on an estrogen-primed endometrium. Early glands show subnuclear glycogen vacuoles. The glands become increasingly tortuous and discharge secretion into their lumina. The stroma becomes edematous, with later predecidual changes around spiral arteries. The spiral arteries lengthen and coil in the functional layer.

questions.text: Describe the maternal and fetal components of the placenta and explain how the histology of the placental barrier supports exchange.
questions.explanation: The fetal capillary blood is normally separated from maternal intervillous blood by the villous interface.
questions.modelAnswer: The maternal component is the decidua basalis and the fetal component is the chorion frondosum. Maternal blood occupies intervillous spaces around chorionic villi containing fetal capillaries. Early in gestation, the interface includes syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, trophoblastic basal lamina, villous connective tissue, and fetal capillary basal lamina and endothelium. The barrier thins as cytotrophoblast becomes discontinuous and fetal capillaries approach the villous surface. Oxygen and nutrients can reach the fetus and wastes can move toward maternal blood. Some drugs also cross.

questions.text: Describe the microscopic appearance of a lactating mammary gland, including its secretory units, ducts, and stroma.
questions.explanation: The lactating gland is dominated by functional secretory alveoli, in contrast to the mostly ductal resting gland.
questions.modelAnswer: Secretory alveoli are numerous and arranged in lobules. Their epithelium is usually simple cuboidal to low columnar and the lumina may contain milk. Myoepithelial cells lie between secretory epithelium and its basal lamina and help expel milk into ducts. Ducts drain the lobules. Adipose and connective tissue are less prominent relative to the expanded glandular tissue.

questions.text: Compare the histology of the vaginal wall and esophageal wall by epithelium, glands, and muscle.
questions.explanation: The epithelial type is similar. Glands and muscle composition distinguish the two walls.
questions.modelAnswer: Both use nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Vaginal epithelial cells may accumulate glycogen, and the vaginal wall lacks intrinsic glands. The vaginal muscular wall is smooth muscle. The esophagus has submucosal mucous glands and a muscularis externa that transitions from skeletal through mixed to smooth muscle along its length.

questions.text: Describe the epithelial lining of the major segments of the loop of Henle and explain how the loop supports urine concentration.
questions.explanation: The medullary gradient allows water reabsorption from collecting ducts when vasopressin increases their water permeability.
questions.modelAnswer: The thick descending segment is the proximal straight tubule, with cuboidal epithelium and a brush border. The thin limbs have simple squamous epithelium. The thick ascending limb has cuboidal epithelium without a prominent brush border. Juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops extending deep into the medulla. Water leaves the descending thin limb, whereas the ascending limb reabsorbs solute with low water permeability. This separation helps establish the medullary osmotic gradient used by collecting ducts.

questions.text: Compare the proximal and distal convoluted tubules by epithelial appearance, apical structures, basal ultrastructure, and main roles.
questions.explanation: A clear distal lumen and lack of a prominent brush border help distinguish the tubules in routine sections.
questions.modelAnswer: Proximal convoluted tubules have relatively tall cuboidal cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct lateral boundaries, and an apical brush border. Their lumina often look irregular. Apical endocytic structures and prominent lateral interdigitations accompany bulk reabsorption. Distal convoluted tubules have lower cuboidal cells with sparse microvilli and no prominent brush border, so their lumina look clearer. Both have basal infoldings associated with mitochondria. The proximal tubule reabsorbs most filtered sodium and water and normally most filtered glucose and amino acids. The early distal tubule selectively reabsorbs sodium chloride.

questions.text: Trace the major renal vessels from the abdominal aorta through the glomerular and postglomerular capillaries to the renal vein.
questions.explanation: An efferent arteriole separates the glomerular capillary bed from its downstream capillary network.
questions.modelAnswer: The abdominal aorta gives rise to the renal artery. Segmental arteries branch into interlobar, arcuate, and cortical radiate arteries. Afferent arterioles supply glomerular capillaries. Efferent arterioles leave those capillaries and supply peritubular networks or, especially in juxtamedullary nephrons, vasa recta. Venous drainage returns through renal venous channels, including cortical radiate, arcuate and interlobar veins, to the renal vein.

questions.text: Describe the layers of the urinary bladder wall and explain how the mucosa changes when the bladder distends.
questions.explanation: The urothelium accommodates distention while maintaining the barrier between urine and the bladder wall.
questions.modelAnswer: The mucosa contains urothelium over a fibroelastic lamina propria. In the relaxed bladder the mucosa is folded and the superficial umbrella cells are dome-shaped. With filling, the folds flatten, the umbrella cells spread and the urothelium looks thinner. The detrusor consists of interlacing smooth-muscle bundles. An outer connective tissue adventitia covers most of the bladder, and a serosa covers its peritoneal surface.

questions.text: How do the microscopic and ultrastructural features of bladder umbrella cells support distention and maintain a urine barrier?
questions.explanation: Membrane trafficking accommodates the changing luminal surface, while plaques and tight junctions maintain the barrier.
questions.modelAnswer: Umbrella cells are large superficial urothelial cells and may be binucleated. They are domed in the relaxed bladder and flatten as it fills. Apical uroplakin plaques contribute to a low-permeability surface. Fusiform vesicles provide a reserve of apical membrane that can be inserted as the surface expands. Tight junctions between neighboring umbrella cells restrict paracellular movement.

questions.text: Which change in collecting-duct principal cells increases water reabsorption in response to vasopressin?
questions.explanation: Vasopressin promotes insertion of aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane of principal cells, increasing water permeability. Proton pumps and pendrin characterize intercalated-cell transport pathways. Sodium-glucose cotransport is a proximal-tubule function.

subjects.name: Physiology
lectureNames: Renal Regulation of Extracellular Volume & Osmolarity

questions.text: Explain how inhibition of renal prostaglandin synthesis by an NSAID can reduce glomerular filtration when effective circulating volume is low.
questions.explanation: The effect is most consequential when renal perfusion already depends on local prostaglandins.
questions.modelAnswer: Local prostaglandins such as PGE2 and prostacyclin help maintain afferent arteriolar dilation when circulating volume is low and vasoconstrictor signals are high. An NSAID inhibits cyclooxygenase and reduces this protective action. Afferent resistance can rise, reducing renal perfusion and glomerular capillary pressure, so filtration may fall.

questions.text: Compare cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons by glomerular location, loop length, postglomerular vessels and contribution to urine concentration.
questions.explanation: The two populations differ by location and associated vascular and tubular architecture.
questions.modelAnswer: Cortical nephron glomeruli lie farther from the corticomedullary junction. Their loops are generally shorter, and their efferent arterioles mainly supply peritubular capillaries. Juxtamedullary glomeruli lie deep in the cortex near the junction. Their long loops extend deep into the medulla and their efferent arterioles give rise to vasa recta. The long loops and vasa recta help establish and preserve the medullary osmotic gradient.

questions.text: Name two structural or hemodynamic characteristics of renal circulation.
questions.explanation: The unusual arrangement of the capillary beds supports filtration upstream and reabsorption downstream.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include high renal blood flow accounting for roughly one fifth to one quarter of resting cardiac output, and an efferent arteriole linking the glomerular and downstream capillary beds. It is also acceptable to contrast the relatively high glomerular capillary pressure with the lower pressure in peritubular capillaries.

questions.text: How do the vasa recta help preserve the renal medullary osmotic gradient?
questions.explanation: The loop of Henle contributes to generating the gradient. The vasa recta help preserve it.
questions.modelAnswer: Hairpin-shaped vasa recta act as passive countercurrent exchangers. As blood descends, it takes up solute and loses water. As it ascends, it returns much of that solute to the medulla and takes up water. Slow flow limits net solute washout while permitting removal of reabsorbed water.

questions.text: What are the two direct hemodynamic determinants of renal blood flow?
questions.explanation: The relationship follows flow equals pressure difference divided by resistance.
questions.modelAnswer: Renal blood flow depends on the pressure gradient from the renal artery to the renal vein and on total renal vascular resistance. At a fixed resistance, a greater pressure gradient increases flow. At a fixed gradient, a greater resistance decreases flow.

questions.text: How can moderate angiotensin II activity help preserve GFR when renal perfusion pressure falls?
questions.explanation: The effect depends on the degree of vasoconstriction and the degree to which renal perfusion falls.
questions.modelAnswer: Moderate angiotensin II activity constricts the efferent arteriole preferentially. This raises downstream resistance and helps maintain glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure despite lower renal plasma flow. With more intense vasoconstriction, reduced flow and rising capillary oncotic pressure can eventually reduce filtration.

questions.text: Define the total glomerular filtration rate.
questions.explanation: GFR measures filtrate formation. It differs from urine flow because most filtered water is reabsorbed.
questions.modelAnswer: It is the volume of fluid filtered from glomerular capillaries into Bowman space by all nephrons of both kidneys per unit time, usually expressed in mL/min.

questions.text: Describe the main constituents of normal glomerular filtrate and compare its macromolecule and cell content with plasma.
questions.explanation: The question concerns the initial filtrate before tubular reabsorption and secretion change its composition.
questions.modelAnswer: The filtrate is primarily water and freely filtered small solutes, including electrolytes, glucose, amino acids and urea. Concentrations of many freely filtered solutes are close to those in plasma water. Blood cells are excluded and large plasma proteins are strongly restricted, so the filtrate has very little protein.

questions.text: List the four Starling pressures at the glomerulus and state which favor or oppose filtration.
questions.explanation: Net filtration pressure reflects the balance across the glomerular wall.
questions.modelAnswer: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure favors movement into Bowman space. Bowman-space hydrostatic pressure and glomerular capillary plasma oncotic pressure oppose filtration. Bowman-space oncotic pressure would favor filtration, but in normal conditions it is negligible because little protein enters the filtrate.

questions.text: State the usual teaching estimates for total GFR and filtration fraction in a healthy resting adult, and define filtration fraction.
questions.explanation: Filtration fraction is dimensionless because it is a ratio of two flow rates measured in the same units.
questions.modelAnswer: Total GFR is commonly estimated at about 125 mL/min as a textbook example. Filtration fraction is GFR divided by renal plasma flow and is approximately one fifth. The actual GFR varies with body size, age and measurement conditions.

questions.text: Name one mediator that relaxes glomerular mesangial cells and explain how relaxation can affect GFR when filtration pressure is fixed.
questions.explanation: This is the surface-area effect of mesangial relaxation, distinct from changes in arteriolar pressure.
questions.modelAnswer: Atrial natriuretic peptide is one example. Relaxation increases the capillary surface area available for filtration, raising the filtration coefficient. If net filtration pressure is unchanged, the increased filtration coefficient raises GFR.

questions.text: Define the renal plasma clearance of a substance.
questions.explanation: Clearance is a calculated volume rate. It does not imply that a physical volume of plasma is entirely emptied of the substance.
questions.modelAnswer: It is the hypothetical volume of plasma from which the kidneys remove the amount of that substance excreted in urine per unit time, typically reported in mL/min.

questions.text: Write the equation for renal clearance and define the quantities needed to calculate it.
questions.explanation: Dividing mass excreted per unit time by mass per unit plasma volume yields a plasma-volume rate.
questions.modelAnswer: Clearance equals urine concentration multiplied by urine flow rate, divided by the plasma concentration of the same substance. Urine and plasma concentrations must use compatible units. If urine flow is in mL/min, clearance is in mL/min.

questions.text: Why is glucose clearance normally close to zero when the filtered load is below the proximal tubule's reabsorptive capacity?
questions.explanation: Glucose clearance increases if filtered glucose exceeds reabsorptive capacity or if proximal glucose transport is impaired.
questions.modelAnswer: Glucose enters the filtrate freely. Proximal tubular sodium–glucose cotransport reabsorbs almost all filtered glucose in this setting, so little or none is excreted. The urinary excretion term in the clearance calculation is therefore close to zero.

questions.text: Why does renal inulin clearance equal glomerular filtration rate?
questions.explanation: This equality is why inulin can be used to measure filtration.
questions.modelAnswer: Inulin is freely filtered, and the tubules neither reabsorb nor secrete it. As a result, the rate of urinary excretion equals the filtered load. Dividing that rate by plasma inulin concentration gives GFR.

questions.text: How is creatinine handled by the kidney, and how does that affect measured creatinine clearance as an estimate of GFR?
questions.explanation: Creatinine is convenient as an endogenous marker, but its clearance is an estimate of filtration.
questions.modelAnswer: Creatinine is freely filtered and a small additional amount is secreted by proximal tubules, with little or no reabsorption. Because urinary excretion includes filtered and secreted creatinine, measured creatinine clearance can overestimate true GFR.

questions.text: Why is the urinary excretion rate of urea usually less than its filtered load?
questions.explanation: Net reabsorption causes urea clearance to be lower than GFR under usual conditions.
questions.modelAnswer: Urea is freely filtered. A substantial portion is passively reabsorbed, especially in the proximal tubule and, when vasopressin is active, in the inner medullary collecting duct. Urea can also reenter parts of the nephron during recycling. The net effect is that less urea is excreted than was initially filtered.

questions.text: Why does low-concentration PAH clearance estimate effective renal plasma flow and usually underestimate total renal plasma flow?
questions.explanation: PAH clearance equals total plasma flow only in the idealized case of complete extraction.
questions.modelAnswer: PAH is filtered and actively secreted into the proximal tubule. At low plasma concentrations, most but not all PAH is removed in one passage through the kidneys. Some PAH remains in renal venous plasma, so the volume effectively cleared is smaller than total renal plasma flow. At higher concentrations secretion can saturate.

questions.text: Describe the apical and basolateral steps of sodium reabsorption in the proximal tubule.
questions.explanation: The apical cotransporters and exchangers are distinct from the primary active basolateral pump.
questions.modelAnswer: Sodium enters proximal tubular cells from the lumen down its electrochemical gradient through apical carriers, including sodium–solute cotransporters and the sodium–hydrogen exchanger. Basolateral sodium–potassium ATPase exports sodium into the interstitium and sustains that inward gradient. Sodium and accompanying water then enter peritubular capillaries.

questions.text: How does the proximal tubule reclaim filtered bicarbonate, and where does active transport contribute?
questions.explanation: The filtered bicarbonate is reclaimed indirectly through carbon dioxide handling and coupled transport.
questions.modelAnswer: Apical sodium–hydrogen exchange secretes hydrogen ions into the lumen, using the gradient maintained by basolateral sodium–potassium ATPase. Luminal hydrogen combines with filtered bicarbonate. Carbonic anhydrase facilitates conversion to carbon dioxide and water. Carbon dioxide enters the cell, where bicarbonate is regenerated and exported across the basolateral membrane.

questions.text: What is splay on the renal glucose titration curve, and why can glucose appear in urine before the whole kidney reaches its glucose transport maximum?
questions.explanation: Threshold is a plasma concentration associated with urinary appearance. Transport maximum is a reabsorptive rate.
questions.modelAnswer: Splay is the gradual bend between the low-load region and the plateau of maximal glucose reabsorption. Individual nephrons and their glucose transporters reach capacity over a range of filtered loads. Some glucose is therefore excreted before aggregate reabsorption reaches its maximum.

questions.text: Explain how the thick ascending limb reabsorbs sodium chloride across its apical and basolateral membranes.
questions.explanation: Salt removal with little accompanying water helps dilute tubular fluid.
questions.modelAnswer: The apical sodium–potassium–2 chloride cotransporter takes up sodium, potassium and chloride from the lumen. Basolateral sodium–potassium ATPase extrudes sodium and maintains the gradient. Chloride leaves through basolateral channels and some potassium recycles through apical channels, supporting continued cotransport.

questions.text: Why can impaired salt reabsorption in the thick ascending limb in Bartter syndrome lead to hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis?
questions.explanation: The distal response to salt wasting contributes to both the potassium deficit and increased bicarbonate in blood.
questions.modelAnswer: Impaired thick-limb salt uptake increases sodium delivery downstream and promotes renal salt loss. Volume contraction activates renin, angiotensin and aldosterone. Distal sodium delivery and aldosterone favor potassium secretion, while enhanced distal hydrogen secretion helps sustain the alkalosis.

questions.text: How does the loop of Henle multiply a transverse osmotic difference into a longitudinal medullary gradient?
questions.explanation: The loop multiplies the gradient. The vasa recta act mainly as a countercurrent exchanger that helps preserve it.
questions.modelAnswer: Ascending-limb NaCl removal with low water permeability creates a local osmotic difference between tubular fluid and interstitium. Water leaves the water-permeable descending limb. Opposing flow continually introduces less concentrated fluid and carries concentrated fluid deeper. Repetition of the local difference along the loop builds a larger corticomedullary gradient.

questions.text: Explain how urea recycling helps maintain inner medullary hyperosmolality during antidiuresis.
questions.explanation: Accumulated inner medullary urea contributes to the osmotic driving force for water reabsorption.
questions.modelAnswer: Water reabsorption concentrates urea in collecting-duct fluid. Vasopressin increases urea permeability in the terminal inner medullary collecting duct, allowing urea to enter the interstitium. Part of that urea moves into thin limbs and returns to the collecting duct, so recycling helps retain urea in the inner medulla.

questions.text: How does vasopressin enable the collecting ducts to concentrate urine?
questions.explanation: Vasopressin allows the collecting ducts to use an existing osmotic gradient.
questions.modelAnswer: Vasopressin activates V2 receptors on collecting-duct principal cells. Signaling promotes apical insertion of aquaporin-2, increasing water permeability and allowing water to follow the medullary osmotic gradient. In the terminal inner medullary collecting duct, vasopressin also increases urea permeability and supports the inner medullary gradient.

questions.text: Distinguish water diuresis from osmotic diuresis by their main mechanisms and expected changes in urinary water and solute excretion.
questions.explanation: Urine volume alone does not identify the mechanism. The solute excretion rate helps distinguish the two.
questions.modelAnswer: Water diuresis occurs when collecting-duct water permeability is low, for example after a water load suppresses vasopressin. Urine is dilute and excess water is excreted without a proportionate increase in solute. Osmotic diuresis occurs when poorly reabsorbed solute remains in the tubule and retains water, so urine flow and solute excretion both rise.

questions.text: Why can measured endogenous creatinine clearance exceed GFR?
questions.explanation: Creatinine enters urine by filtration and tubular secretion. The secreted amount increases urinary excretion above the filtered load, so creatinine clearance can overestimate GFR.
options: Tubular reabsorption lowers urinary creatinine excretion
Tubular secretion adds creatinine to the filtered load
Protein binding increases the amount freely filtered
Tubular metabolism increases the plasma concentration
Reduced urine flow increases the amount excreted per minute

questions.text: A patient's inulin clearance is 25 mL/min. What does this measure?
questions.explanation: Inulin is freely filtered and undergoes negligible tubular secretion or reabsorption. Its clearance estimates GFR, but the measurement alone cannot tell how many nephrons are functioning.
options: Renal plasma flow of about 25 mL/min
Total renal blood flow of about 25 mL/min
Tubular inulin secretion of about 25 mL/min
Glomerular filtration rate of about 25 mL/min

questions.text: What happens when the filtered phosphate load rises beyond tubular reabsorptive capacity?
questions.explanation: Once phosphate transport approaches its maximum, additional filtered phosphate cannot all be reclaimed. More reaches the urine.
options: Tubular reabsorption rises in proportion to the load
Urinary phosphate excretion falls below baseline
Tubular phosphate reabsorptive capacity becomes unlimited

questions.text: In the textbook's reference model, what is the approximate osmolality of fluid leaving the ascending limb of the loop of Henle?
questions.explanation: Solute leaves the ascending limb while its wall has low water permeability. The tubular fluid becomes dilute. In the textbook example, it reaches about 100 mOsm/kg H₂O at the outlet.

questions.text: Which signaling sequence increases apical water permeability in collecting duct principal cells after vasopressin binds?
questions.explanation: Vasopressin activates basolateral V2 receptors. Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP and activating PKA. This promotes AQP2 insertion into the apical membrane, where it increases water permeability.
options: V1 receptor → Gq signaling → basolateral AQP2 insertion
V2 receptor → decreased cAMP → apical AQP2 insertion
V2 receptor → increased cAMP → basolateral AQP2 insertion
V2 receptor → increased cAMP → apical AQP2 insertion
V1 receptor → Gq signaling → apical ENaC insertion

questions.text: Peritubular capillary oncotic and hydrostatic pressures are 32 and 13 mmHg. Interstitial hydrostatic and oncotic pressures are 6 and 15 mmHg. What is the net pressure driving reabsorption?
questions.explanation: Capillary oncotic and interstitial hydrostatic pressures favor uptake. Capillary hydrostatic and interstitial oncotic pressures oppose it. Subtracting the opposing forces gives (32 + 6) − (13 + 15) = 10 mmHg inward.

questions.text: GFR rises while renal plasma flow and incoming plasma protein concentration remain constant. Which sequence favors proximal tubular reabsorption?
questions.explanation: At constant plasma flow, a higher GFR filters a greater fraction of that flow. The proteins left in postglomerular blood are more concentrated, increasing peritubular oncotic pressure and favoring reabsorption.
options: Lower filtration fraction → lower peritubular oncotic pressure
Higher filtration fraction → higher peritubular oncotic pressure
Higher filtration fraction → lower peritubular oncotic pressure
Higher peritubular hydrostatic pressure → greater capillary uptake
Higher interstitial oncotic pressure → greater capillary uptake

questions.text: A freely filtered solute has lower renal clearance than inulin measured at the same time. What is its net tubular handling?
questions.explanation: Inulin clearance estimates GFR. A freely filtered solute with lower clearance is excreted at a rate below its filtered load, so tubular reabsorption exceeds secretion.
options: Complete secretion of the filtered load

questions.text: In the course model, what is the approximate lower limit of tubular fluid pH generated by distal proton secretion?
questions.explanation: The distal nephron can acidify tubular fluid to about pH 4.5. Ammonia and phosphate bind secreted protons, allowing more acid to leave in the urine without requiring a lower tubular fluid pH.

questions.text: Which relationship describes urinary sodium excretion when tubular sodium secretion is negligible?
questions.explanation: Sodium is filtered at the glomerulus. Tubular reabsorption returns some of the filtered sodium to blood. With negligible tubular secretion, the amount left is the amount excreted.

questions.text: During dietary potassium depletion, which collecting-duct cell and apical transporter help conserve potassium?
questions.explanation: Apical H⁺/K⁺-ATPase in alpha-intercalated cells takes up potassium from tubular fluid in exchange for secreting hydrogen ions. This helps conserve potassium during depletion.

questions.text: If the tubules reabsorb 98–99% of the filtered calcium and do not secrete it, how much is excreted per 100 filtered units?
questions.explanation: Without tubular secretion, excretion equals filtration minus reabsorption. Reabsorbing 98–99 out of 100 filtered units leaves 1–2 units for excretion.

questions.text: The course model describes 90% of plasma phosphate as filterable and roughly 80–85% as reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. What does the proximal percentage refer to?
questions.explanation: The filterable fraction uses total plasma phosphate as its denominator. Proximal fractional reabsorption instead uses the phosphate that has already entered the glomerular filtrate.
options: All phosphate in the circulating blood
The phosphate fraction bound to plasma proteins
The phosphate load that entered the glomerular filtrate
Urinary phosphate excretion measured over one day
The phosphate load already reabsorbed beyond the proximal tubule

questions.text: What are the direct effects of parathyroid hormone on distal tubular calcium reabsorption and proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption?
questions.explanation: PTH increases distal calcium reabsorption and inhibits proximal phosphate reabsorption. These are tubular transport effects. Net urinary calcium also depends on the calcium load filtered at the glomerulus.
options: Calcium stays unchanged and phosphate increases

questions.text: Which molecule is the common starting substrate for synthesis of all steroid hormones?
questions.explanation: The first step in steroidogenesis converts cholesterol to pregnenolone. Cholesterol is the starting substrate, and pregnenolone is the first steroid intermediate.
questions.modelAnswer: Cholesterol.

questions.text: Name the three principal substrates for renal cortical gluconeogenesis listed in the course's renal metabolism chapter.
questions.explanation: Renal cortical cells can make glucose from noncarbohydrate precursors. The course chapter highlights lactate, glycerol and glutamine.
questions.modelAnswer: Lactate, glycerol and glutamine.

questions.text: Name three distinct ways the kidney handles glucose or contributes to glucose homeostasis.
questions.explanation: Reabsorption reclaims existing glucose from the filtrate. Gluconeogenesis increases the circulating supply by making new glucose.
questions.modelAnswer: It uses glucose to meet energy needs, reabsorbs filtered glucose into the circulation, and synthesizes and releases glucose by gluconeogenesis during fasting.

questions.text: Name the three renal endocrine products listed in the course chapter on renal metabolism.
questions.explanation: Erythropoietin supports red-cell production, the kidney activates vitamin D to calcitriol, and renin initiates the renin–angiotensin system.
questions.modelAnswer: Erythropoietin, calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), and renin.

questions.text: Name the three glomerular basement membrane proteins listed in the renal metabolism chapter.
questions.explanation: Type IV collagen and laminin form basement membrane networks. Nidogen, also called entactin, is an associated basement membrane protein.
questions.modelAnswer: Type IV collagen, laminin and nidogen (entactin).

questions.text: An ovarian cyst removed from a 27-year-old woman contains a tooth, hair, and sebaceous material. From which cell lineage does this lesion arise?
questions.explanation: A mature cystic teratoma is an ovarian germ cell tumor. Its differentiated tissues can include skin appendages and teeth.
questions.modelAnswer: Germ cells.

questions.text: A uterine tissue section shows endometrial glands and stroma deep within the myometrium. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Adenomyosis places endometrial glands and stroma within uterine smooth muscle. Extrauterine implants are a distinct finding of endometriosis.
questions.modelAnswer: Adenomyosis.

questions.text: Which prostatic lobe lies between the upper prostatic urethra and the ejaculatory ducts?
questions.explanation: The median lobe lies between the upper prostatic urethra and the ejaculatory ducts. The posterior lobe is below the ducts, while the anterior lobe is ventral to the urethra.

questions.text: Which pair of lumbar ventral rami contributes to the lumbosacral trunk?
questions.explanation: The lumbosacral trunk contains contributions from L4 and L5. Upper sacral ventral rami join it in forming the sacral plexus.

questions.text: Which landmark marks the middle of the three normal ureteric constrictions?
questions.explanation: The middle narrowing is at the pelvic brim near the common iliac bifurcation. The proximal narrowing is at the ureteropelvic junction and the distal narrowing is within the bladder wall.
options: The tip of the ischial spine
The inner surface of the bladder

questions.text: Which embryonic structure gives rise to the uterine tubes?
questions.explanation: The cranial portions of the paramesonephric ducts remain unfused and form the uterine tubes. Their caudal portions fuse to form the uterovaginal canal.

questions.text: Both kidneys are low in position, and a band of renal tissue joins their lower poles. Which developmental anomaly explains this finding?
questions.explanation: Fusion of the lower renal poles produces a horseshoe kidney. Its ascent can be limited by the root of the inferior mesenteric artery.

questions.text: During urinary tract development, the ureteric bud grows out from which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation: The ureteric bud arises from the caudal mesonephric duct. It grows toward the metanephric mesenchyme, which contributes the nephron rather than the bud.

questions.text: Which structure lies anterior to the left kidney across the omental bursa?
questions.explanation: The gastric area of the left kidney is covered by peritoneum of the omental bursa. The spleen lies across the greater sac, and the pancreatic, suprarenal, and colic contact areas lack a peritoneal covering.

questions.text: Which ligament runs from the apex of the adult urinary bladder to the umbilicus?
questions.explanation: The median umbilical ligament is the remnant of the urachus. It connects the bladder apex to the umbilicus. The medial umbilical ligament is associated with an obliterated umbilical artery.

questions.text: Which embryonic structure persists in the female as Gartner’s duct?
questions.explanation: Gartner’s duct is a remnant of the mesonephric duct. Some mesonephric tubules persist separately as the epoophoron and paroophoron.
options: Vesical part of the urogenital sinus

questions.text: A duplicated upper collecting system drains through two ureteric limbs that join before reaching the bladder. Which developmental event explains this anatomy?
questions.explanation: Partial splitting of a ureteric bud produces a bifid ureter. The two limbs share a distal ureter and therefore do not enter the bladder through separate openings.
options: Failed incorporation of the caudal mesonephric duct
Premature regression of the ureteric bud
Failure of fusion between the two metanephric masses
Partial splitting of one ureteric bud
Complete splitting of one ureteric bud

questions.text: Where is the Golgi apparatus located in a macula densa cell relative to its nucleus?
questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus lies between the nucleus and the basal border. The nucleus is positioned toward the lumen in these epithelial cells.

questions.text: Which structures are directly bridged by the glomerular slit diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The slit diaphragm spans the gap between adjacent podocyte foot processes. Capillary endothelial fenestrations are distinct from these epithelial slits.

questions.text: Which microscopic feature distinguishes the proximal convoluted tubule from the distal convoluted tubule?
questions.explanation: The proximal tubule has numerous apical microvilli that form a brush border. The distal tubule has fewer microvilli and lacks a prominent brush border.

questions.text: The glomerular basement membrane forms by fusion of the basal laminae of which two cell types?
questions.explanation: The basal laminae of the glomerular capillary endothelium and podocytes fuse to form the shared membrane of the filtration barrier.
options: Mesangial cells and glomerular endothelial cells
Parietal epithelial cells and mesangial cells
Proximal tubular cells and parietal epithelial cells

lectureNames: Renal Regulation of Extracellular Volume & Osmolarity

questions.text: Which measurement estimates the maximum capacity of the proximal tubule to secrete para-aminohippurate (PAH)?
questions.explanation: At a plasma PAH concentration that saturates its transporters, the maximal secretion rate is the transport maximum. It is calculated as PAH excretion rate minus its filtered load. Low-concentration PAH clearance estimates effective renal plasma flow.

questions.text: Which spinous processes mark the upper and lower horizontal boundaries of Morris’s rectangle for the kidney?
questions.explanation: The course surface-marking diagram places the upper boundary at the T11 spinous process and the lower boundary at L3.

questions.text: What is the approximate length of one adult ureter?
questions.explanation: An adult ureter is about 25–30 cm long. Its abdominal and pelvic portions make up roughly equal lengths.

questions.text: What is the immediate nitrogen-containing product released when renal glutaminase converts glutamine to glutamate?
questions.explanation: Glutaminase releases ammonium when it hydrolyses glutamine to glutamate. Renal ammonia can buffer secreted hydrogen ions in tubular fluid, allowing acid excretion as ammonium.

questions.text: Juxtaglomerular granular cells are a modified form of which cell type?
questions.explanation: Juxtaglomerular granular cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the arteriolar wall, mainly in the afferent arteriole. They synthesize and release renin.

questions.text: Which proteins form plaques in the apical membrane of urothelial umbrella cells?
questions.explanation: Uroplakins form the plaques of the apical asymmetric unit membrane. The plaques and tight junctions help maintain the urothelial permeability barrier.

questions.text: In a healthy adult whose plasma glucose is below the renal threshold, which substance has the lowest renal clearance?
questions.explanation: Filtered glucose is almost completely reabsorbed below the renal threshold, so its clearance is normally close to zero. Urea, creatinine and inulin are excreted in measurable amounts.

questions.text: Which isolated change directly stimulates renin release through the intrarenal pressure-sensing mechanism?
questions.explanation: Reduced stretch in the afferent arteriolar wall stimulates nearby granular cells to release renin. Low macula densa sodium chloride delivery and beta-1 sympathetic stimulation are distinct signals.
options: Increased sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa

questions.text: Which segment of the loop of Henle has high water permeability and little sodium chloride reabsorption in the course model?
questions.explanation: The thin descending limb preferentially loses water. The ascending limbs instead reabsorb sodium chloride and have low water permeability.

questions.text: Which statement correctly describes the renal handling of inulin?
questions.explanation: Inulin is freely filtered. The tubules neither secrete nor reabsorb it, so its clearance measures GFR.
options: Filtered and actively secreted in the proximal tubule
Secreted by the tubules without glomerular filtration

questions.text: Which of these conditions is most likely to cause normal-anion-gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis?
questions.explanation: Loss of bicarbonate in diarrheal stool lowers plasma bicarbonate. The relative rise in chloride preserves a normal anion gap.

questions.text: Which alteration explains isolated renal glucosuria in a person with normal plasma glucose?
questions.explanation: A lower proximal tubular glucose threshold allows glucose to be excreted at plasma concentrations that would normally permit near-complete reabsorption.
options: Reduced filtration of glucose at the glomerulus

questions.text: The afferent arterioles dilate while perfusion pressure and efferent resistance stay constant. How do renal blood flow and glomerular capillary pressure change?
questions.explanation: Afferent dilation lowers resistance to blood entering the glomerular capillaries. With efferent resistance and perfusion pressure unchanged, flow and capillary pressure rise.
options: Flow rises and capillary pressure falls
Flow falls and capillary pressure rises

questions.text: A renal calculus is hard, dark brown, rough and radiopaque. Which composition best fits this description?
questions.explanation: The course describes calcium oxalate stones as hard, dark, spiky and radiopaque. These features support the exam identification.

questions.text: Lymphatic vessels from an ovary follow the ovarian vessels primarily to which lymph nodes?
questions.explanation: The primary ovarian lymphatic route follows the ovarian vessels to the lumbar para-aortic nodes.

questions.text: In 17α-hydroxylase deficiency, which accumulated steroid contributes to mineralocorticoid hypertension?
questions.explanation: Loss of 17α-hydroxylase activity favors production of 11-deoxycorticosterone. Its mineralocorticoid action promotes sodium retention and suppresses renin.

questions.text: An adult has arthritis, blue-black scleral pigmentation and urine that darkens on standing. Which metabolite accumulates in the urine?
questions.explanation: In alkaptonuria, deficient homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase causes homogentisic acid accumulation and excretion. Its oxidation darkens urine on standing, and tissue deposits cause ochronosis.

questions.text: What two properties determine the glomerular ultrafiltration coefficient, Kf?
questions.explanation: Kf equals filtration surface area multiplied by hydraulic permeability. The hydrostatic and oncotic pressures determine the separate net filtration pressure term.
options: Hydrostatic pressure and plasma oncotic pressure
Renal plasma flow and glomerular filtration fraction
Afferent arteriolar resistance and efferent arteriolar resistance

questions.text: Which renal response helps compensate for a sustained rise in arterial carbon dioxide?
questions.explanation: Higher carbon dioxide promotes hydrogen ion secretion by renal tubular cells. Renal acid handling and bicarbonate retention help compensate for respiratory acidosis.

questions.text: Which substance released by the kidney in response to hypoxia stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow?
questions.explanation: Hypoxia stimulates renal erythropoietin release, which increases red blood cell production in the bone marrow. The other listed renal products regulate different processes.

questions.text: A plot of carrier-mediated renal transport against substrate concentration levels off at high concentrations. What does the plateau represent?
questions.explanation: At transport maximum, the relevant tubular carriers are saturated, so the rate cannot increase further. Renal threshold instead describes the plasma concentration where urinary appearance begins.
options: Amount delivered by filtration per minute
Plasma concentration at first urinary appearance
Amount excreted in final urine per minute
Maximum tubular reabsorption or secretion rate
Volume of plasma cleared per minute

questions.text: A patient has recurrent renal stones and increased urinary excretion of cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine. Which defect explains this pattern?
questions.explanation: Cystinuria impairs renal tubular reabsorption of cystine and the dibasic amino acids. Excess urinary cystine can precipitate and form stones.
options: Failure of lysosomal cystine export into the cytosol
Generalised failure of proximal tubular reabsorption of solutes
Impaired apical uptake of cystine and dibasic amino acids
Impaired uptake of neutral amino acids by renal tubules
Failure of proximal tubular reclamation of filtered bicarbonate

questions.text: Which isolated change would increase glomerular filtration rate?
questions.explanation: Plasma oncotic pressure opposes filtration. Lowering it increases net filtration pressure and GFR when the other determinants are fixed.
options: Increased hydrostatic pressure in Bowman’s space

questions.text: A freely filtered substance has a renal clearance greater than that of inulin but less than that of PAH. What can be inferred about its tubular handling?
questions.explanation: For a freely filtered substance, clearance greater than GFR means excretion exceeds the filtered load. Tubular secretion therefore exceeds reabsorption, even though the individual transport rates are unknown.
options: All of the filtered solute is reabsorbed
The tubules neither secrete nor reabsorb it

questions.text: Which process in the vasa recta helps preserve the renal medullary osmotic gradient?
questions.explanation: Solutes enter the descending vasa recta from the medullary interstitium and diffuse back out along the ascending vasa recta. This passive exchange limits solute washout.
options: Active sodium chloride transport out of descending vessels
Passive urea movement out of descending vessels
Active urea transport into ascending vessels
Passive sodium chloride movement out of ascending vessels
Passive sodium chloride movement into ascending vessels

questions.text: A cervical carcinoma compresses both distal ureters. Which structural change is expected in the kidneys if the obstruction persists?
questions.explanation: Persistent blockage of urinary outflow transmits pressure upstream and dilates the collecting systems. This is hydronephrosis.
options: Segmental infarction of the renal cortex
Calcification of the renal papillary tips
Dilation of renal pelves and calyces

questions.text: Which description identifies the macula densa at the vascular pole of a renal corpuscle?
questions.explanation: The macula densa is a specialized, densely packed patch of distal tubular epithelial cells at the vascular pole. It senses tubular NaCl delivery.
options: Widely spaced cells lining Bowman’s capsule
Modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole

questions.text: Which enzyme catalyzes conversion of luminal carbonic acid into carbon dioxide and water during proximal bicarbonate reclamation?
questions.explanation: Luminal carbonic anhydrase facilitates CO₂ formation from carbonic acid. CO₂ enters the cell, where intracellular carbonic anhydrase helps regenerate bicarbonate.

questions.text: Which change stimulates granular cells of the afferent arteriole to release renin directly through an adrenergic pathway?
questions.explanation: Sympathetic β1 activation stimulates renin release from juxtaglomerular cells. Increased afferent pressure, increased distal NaCl delivery and angiotensin II feedback tend to suppress renin.
options: Higher sodium delivery at the macula densa
Higher pressure within the afferent arteriole

questions.text: For each independent situation, predict the change in glomerular filtration rate and explain the mechanism. Assume other determinants remain unchanged unless the situation affects them directly.
questions.explanation: The three scenarios test separate determinants of filtration.
questions.modelAnswer: The three scenarios test separate determinants of filtration.

subQuestions.text: Liver disease causes a fall in glomerular plasma oncotic pressure. What happens to GFR if renal perfusion and other filtration factors stay fixed?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: GFR increases in this isolated model. Lower glomerular capillary oncotic pressure reduces the force opposing filtration.
subQuestions.explanation: Liver disease can also impair renal perfusion. The question isolates the fall in oncotic pressure.

subQuestions.text: An enlarged prostate obstructs bladder outflow and the resulting pressure is transmitted back to the nephrons. What happens to GFR?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: GFR falls. Increased hydrostatic pressure in Bowman space opposes glomerular filtration.
subQuestions.explanation: Obstruction can raise pressure downstream from the glomerulus and reduce net filtration pressure.

subQuestions.text: The efferent arteriole constricts severely while the afferent resistance and upstream pressure stay fixed. What happens to GFR?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: GFR falls with sufficiently severe constriction. The fall in renal plasma flow raises glomerular capillary oncotic pressure enough to outweigh the initial rise in hydraulic pressure.
subQuestions.explanation: Mild or moderate efferent constriction can increase GFR. The question specifies sufficiently severe constriction.

questions.text: Describe how the proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs filtered phosphate and explain the effect of parathyroid hormone on this process.
questions.explanation: Apical phosphate uptake depends on the sodium gradient. Reducing the activity of sodium–phosphate cotransporters leaves more phosphate in the tubular fluid.
questions.modelAnswer: Most filtered phosphate is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by apical sodium–phosphate cotransport. Parathyroid hormone inhibits proximal phosphate reabsorption, increasing phosphate excretion in urine.

questions.text: Explain how glomerular crescents form in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
questions.explanation: Crescent formation is a shared response to severe capillary injury across several etiologies of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
questions.modelAnswer: Severe injury disrupts the glomerular capillary wall and basement membrane, allowing plasma proteins and fibrin to enter Bowman space. Parietal epithelial cells proliferate and macrophages enter. The cells and fibrin accumulate in a crescent and may compress the glomerular tuft.

questions.text: List two distinct complications of renal calculi.
questions.explanation: Hydroureter and hydronephrosis can both result from obstruction. Treat them as one complication mechanism when scoring two distinct examples.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include hematuria from mucosal injury, urinary tract infection, and obstruction with hydroureter or hydronephrosis. Give any two distinct complications.

questions.text: Name the commonest primary glomerular lesion causing nephrotic syndrome in children and describe its light and electron microscopic appearance.
questions.explanation: The diagnostic ultrastructural change is visible even when the glomeruli look normal by light microscopy.
questions.modelAnswer: Minimal change disease. Glomeruli appear essentially normal on light microscopy. Electron microscopy shows diffuse podocyte foot process effacement.

questions.text: List the arterial sources that contribute to the blood supply of the abdominal ureter.
questions.explanation: These sources feed a longitudinal arterial network along the abdominal ureter.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of the renal artery, abdominal aorta, gonadal artery, and common iliac artery.

questions.text: Explain how afferent and efferent arteriolar resistance affect glomerular filtration and the downstream capillary beds.
questions.explanation: Both resistances affect flow and filtration. Moderate efferent constriction can raise capillary pressure, while severe constriction can reduce GFR as renal plasma flow falls and capillary oncotic pressure rises.
questions.modelAnswer: Changing afferent resistance helps autoregulate renal blood flow and GFR. Efferent resistance helps maintain glomerular capillary pressure. Downstream, low peritubular capillary hydrostatic pressure favors fluid uptake, and slow vasa recta flow reduces washout of medullary solutes.

questions.text: In a male pelvis, onto which surface of the urinary bladder does the peritoneum reflect from the rectum to form the rectovesical pouch?
questions.explanation: Peritoneum reflects from the rectum onto the superior bladder surface, creating the rectovesical pouch. The inferolateral surfaces are extraperitoneal.
options: Anterior aspect at the pubic symphysis
Inferior aspect at the bladder neck

questions.text: A healthy young woman develops uncomplicated cystitis after intercourse. The urine isolate is a motile, lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: E. coli is the most common cause of uncomplicated cystitis and fits the motile lactose-fermenting rod description. K. pneumoniae is typically nonmotile, P. mirabilis does not ferment lactose, and S. saprophyticus is a Gram-positive coccus.

questions.text: Which nerve arises from the lumbar plexus rather than the sacral plexus?
questions.explanation: The obturator nerve arises from L2–L4 in the lumbar plexus. The nerve to obturator internus is a separate branch of the sacral plexus.

questions.text: In which compartment are the bulbourethral glands themselves located?
questions.explanation: The bulbourethral glands lie in the deep perineal pouch. Their ducts pierce the perineal membrane and open into the proximal spongy urethra.

questions.text: Name the three arteries carried in the spermatic cord.
questions.explanation: The three arteries supply the testis, ductus deferens, and cremasteric region. The pampiniform plexus is venous.
questions.modelAnswer: The testicular artery, the artery to the ductus deferens, and the cremasteric artery.

questions.text: Describe the effect of rising ovarian estrogen on the endometrium in the late follicular phase.
questions.explanation: The late ovarian follicular phase corresponds to the uterine proliferative phase.
questions.modelAnswer: Estrogen stimulates regeneration and proliferation of the functional endometrium after menstruation. The surface epithelium and stroma proliferate, uterine glands lengthen, and spiral arteries grow as the functional layer thickens. The prominent glandular secretory changes follow ovulation under progesterone.

questions.text: Which artery usually arises from the posterior division of the internal iliac artery?
questions.explanation: The superior gluteal artery usually arises from the posterior division. The internal pudendal, inferior gluteal and superior vesical arteries usually arise from the anterior division.

questions.text: What lies between the superior fascial layer of the urogenital diaphragm and the perineal membrane?
questions.explanation: The deep perineal pouch lies between the named layers. The ischiorectal fossa belongs to the anal triangle. Colles fascia is membranous superficial perineal fascia, continuous anteriorly with abdominal Scarpa fascia. The superficial perineal pouch lies below the perineal membrane.

questions.text: Which of the following is not a content of the spermatic cord?
questions.explanation: The testicular, cremasteric and deferential arteries and pampiniform venous plexus are cord constituents. The enumerated nerve components are the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve and sympathetic plexuses. The ilioinguinal nerve accompanies the cord in the canal without belonging to its contents.

questions.text: Which subdivision of the broad ligament lies between the uterine tube and the ovary?
questions.explanation: The mesosalpinx is the part associated with the uterine tube. The mesovarium attaches to the ovary, and the mesometrium lies alongside the uterus.

questions.text: Which anterior abdominal wall layer gives rise to the internal spermatic fascia?
questions.explanation: The internal spermatic fascia derives from transversalis fascia. The cremasteric covering derives from internal oblique, and the external spermatic fascia from the external oblique aponeurosis.

questions.text: Into which vessel does the left testicular vein normally empty?
questions.explanation: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein. The right testicular vein usually drains directly into the inferior vena cava.

questions.text: Which of the following structures lies in the superficial perineal pouch in males?
questions.explanation: The bulb forms part of the root of the penis and lies below the perineal membrane in the superficial pouch. The bulbourethral glands themselves lie in the deep pouch, although their ducts enter the superficial pouch.

questions.text: Which artery typically arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery?
questions.explanation: The obturator artery is usually a parietal branch of the anterior division. The iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal arteries usually arise from the posterior division. The superior rectal artery continues from the inferior mesenteric artery.

questions.text: In the five-lobe description of the prostate, which lobe lies behind the prostatic urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts?
questions.explanation: The posterior lobe lies behind the urethra and below the ejaculatory ducts. The median lobe lies between the upper prostatic urethra and the ducts.

questions.text: Which histological feature identifies the macula densa at the vascular pole of a renal corpuscle?
questions.explanation: Macula densa cells form a closely packed epithelial patch where the distal nephron passes the vascular pole. Granular cells are modified smooth-muscle cells of the arteriolar wall.
options: Contractile cells between adjacent glomerular capillary loops
Granule-containing cells in the afferent arteriolar wall
Closely packed tubular epithelial cells with crowded nuclei
Flattened epithelial cells lining the parietal capsule

questions.text: The vas deferens is characterised by which of the following features?
questions.explanation: The vas deferens has a conspicuously thick smooth-muscle wall, classically with inner longitudinal, middle circular and outer longitudinal layers. It has a narrow lumen, a stereociliated pseudostratified lining and an adventitia.
options: It is lined with transitional epithelium

questions.text: Which structure forms the blood–testis barrier within the seminiferous epithelium?
questions.explanation: Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells divide the seminiferous epithelium into basal and adluminal compartments, limiting passage between them.
options: Basement membrane of a seminiferous tubule
Adherens junctions between adjacent myoid cells
Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells
Tight junctions between interstitial Leydig cells

questions.text: Which Sertoli-cell secretion helps maintain a high testosterone concentration in the lumen of seminiferous tubules?
questions.explanation: Androgen-binding protein binds testosterone within seminiferous tubules, helping maintain its local concentration. Inhibin instead participates in feedback control of FSH secretion.

lectureNames: Renal Regulation of Extracellular Volume & Osmolarity

questions.text: At rest, what approximate fraction of an adult's cardiac output reaches both kidneys?
questions.explanation: Both kidneys receive approximately one fifth to one quarter of resting cardiac output. Renal plasma flow is lower than whole-blood renal flow because it excludes the cellular fraction.

questions.text: Which basolateral transporter maintains the sodium gradient that drives apical sodium uptake in the proximal tubule?
questions.explanation: The basolateral sodium-potassium ATPase expels intracellular sodium using ATP. This keeps intracellular sodium low enough to support secondary active transport on the apical side.

questions.text: Which structure is formed when the two sinovaginal bulbs fuse?
questions.explanation: Fusion of the sinovaginal bulbs forms the solid vaginal plate. Canalization later contributes to the vaginal lumen. The uterovaginal canal instead develops from the fused paramesonephric ducts.

questions.text: After the initial stimulatory phase, how does continuous leuprolide lower gonadal steroid production?
questions.explanation: Continuous GnRH agonist exposure desensitizes pituitary gonadotropes. LH and FSH fall after the initial rise, reducing gonadal steroid production.
options: It blocks androgen receptors in target tissues
It inhibits conversion of testosterone to DHT
It reduces pituitary LH and FSH release

questions.text: Which signaling change in cavernosal smooth muscle directly follows nitric oxide release during erection?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide activates soluble guanylyl cyclase, raising cGMP and relaxing cavernosal smooth muscle. Phosphodiesterase 5 breaks down cGMP.
options: Increased cGMP through guanylyl cyclase activation
Increased cAMP through adrenergic receptor activation
Reduced cAMP through adenylyl cyclase inhibition

questions.text: Which two structures bound the interval occupied by the seminal vesicles, from anterior to posterior?
questions.explanation: The seminal vesicles lie posterior to the base of the bladder and anterior to the rectum. Each duct joins the ductus deferens to form an ejaculatory duct.

questions.text: Which change after delivery removes the placental hormonal restraint on copious milk secretion?
questions.explanation: Expulsion of the placenta lowers circulating estrogen and progesterone. This permits prolactin to support copious milk synthesis. Oxytocin helps eject milk already made.
options: Rise in maternal progesterone and estrogen
Fall in maternal estrogen and progesterone
Rise in placental human chorionic gonadotropin
Fall in maternal prolactin and oxytocin

questions.text: Which congenital infection can cause nonimmune fetal hydrops by suppressing fetal erythropoiesis?
questions.explanation: Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid precursors. Suppression of fetal red-cell production can cause severe fetal anemia, which can in turn lead to nonimmune hydrops.

questions.text: In Alport syndrome, which basement-membrane protein is altered in the glomerulus with basket-weave lamellation?
questions.explanation: Pathogenic variants affecting the alpha chains of type IV collagen disrupt the glomerular basement membrane. It can show alternating thinning and thickening with lamellation on electron microscopy.

questions.text: A renal biopsy shows glomerular crescents and smooth linear IgG staining along the glomerular capillary walls. Which antibody specificity explains this staining pattern?
questions.explanation: Anti-GBM antibodies bind targets distributed along the glomerular basement membrane. This produces linear IgG staining. ANCA-associated disease is usually pauci-immune, and membranous disease shows granular deposits.

questions.text: A patient develops acute kidney injury after starting a penicillin antibiotic. Biopsy shows interstitial edema with an eosinophil-rich infiltrate and tubulitis. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.explanation: Drug-induced acute tubulointerstitial nephritis can present with interstitial edema, inflammatory cells including eosinophils, and tubulitis. The lesion is centered in the interstitium and tubules.

questions.text: Which change helps superficial urothelial cells expand their apical surface as the bladder fills?
questions.explanation: Fusiform vesicles in umbrella cells can fuse with the luminal membrane as the bladder distends. Tight junctions remain part of the urine barrier.
options: Deposition of a thicker basal lamina
Migration of intermediate cells into the lumen

questions.text: A patient has homogeneous gray vaginal discharge and a fishy odor. Microscopy shows squamous epithelial cells coated with bacteria. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.explanation: Bacteria coating squamous epithelial cells create clue cells. Together with a homogeneous discharge and amine odor, this supports bacterial vaginosis, a polymicrobial shift in vaginal flora.

questions.text: A pregnant patient has fever, flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness and pyuria with white-cell casts. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.explanation: Fever and flank tenderness with pyuria support upper urinary tract infection. White-cell casts localize inflammation to the kidney and can be seen in acute pyelonephritis.

questions.text: Which of the following parts of the sperm is surrounded by mitochondria?
questions.explanation: A helical mitochondrial sheath surrounds the axoneme and its associated structures in the middle piece. The principal piece instead has a fibrous sheath.

questions.text: Which pelvic muscle lies immediately posterior to the sacral plexus?
questions.explanation: The sacral plexus lies on the anterior surface of piriformis. The sciatic nerve usually leaves the pelvis below piriformis through the greater sciatic foramen.

questions.text: A 78 year old was admitted to the hospital due to acute urinary tract obstruction. For the past few years, he has had recurrent bouts of cystitis. Two days before being admitted to the hospital, he was not able to urinate at all. What is the probable cause of bladder outlet obstruction in this case?
questions.explanation: Periurethral nodules in benign prostatic hyperplasia can narrow the prostatic urethra and cause urinary retention. Residual urine can contribute to recurrent cystitis. The vignette supplies no specific evidence of a stricture or malignancy.
options: Urothelial cell carcinoma of the bladder

questions.text: An 8 year old boy is brought to the physician by his parents who noticed the appearance of puberty symptoms on him. Physical examination revealed enlargement of the external genitalia and facial hair. Which of the following neoplasms is the most likely cause of precocious puberty in this patient?
questions.explanation: A functioning Leydig cell tumor can secrete androgens and cause early virilization. The characteristic mechanism is peripheral androgen excess.

questions.text: In a patient with longstanding bladder outlet obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia, which finding follows directly from sustained upstream urinary pressure?
questions.explanation: Persistent outflow resistance can transmit pressure back to both ureters and renal collecting systems. This can dilate the ureters and renal pelvicalyceal systems.
options: Unilateral dilation of a renal vein
A focal abscess limited to the prostate

questions.text: A bladder tumor contains invasive nests with intercellular bridges and keratin pearls. Extensive sampling shows no urothelial carcinoma component. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.explanation: Keratin pearls and intercellular bridges support squamous differentiation. Invasion and absence of a urothelial component in the sampled tumor support primary squamous cell carcinoma rather than urothelial carcinoma with focal squamous differentiation.

questions.text: Which of the following gives rise to the labia minora?
questions.explanation: The urethral folds remain unfused and form the labia minora. The labioscrotal swellings form the labia majora, and the genital tubercle contributes to the clitoris.

questions.text: Which of the following is related to the posterior surface of the prostate?
questions.explanation: The rectum is posterior to the prostate, separated by the rectoprostatic fascia. The bladder is superior to the gland and levator ani lies inferolaterally.

questions.text: Which embryonic structure gives rise to the seminal vesicles?
questions.explanation: The seminal vesicles form as outgrowths from the distal mesonephric ducts. Prostatic glands instead develop from the urogenital sinus.

questions.text: Explain how combined oral contraceptives prevent pregnancy.
questions.explanation: The principal effect is inhibition of ovulation, with cervical mucus changes adding a separate barrier to sperm.
questions.modelAnswer: Estrogen and progestin provide negative feedback on gonadotropin release, reducing follicular development and preventing the midcycle LH surge and ovulation. Progestin thickens cervical mucus, making sperm penetration more difficult. The endometrium also changes during use.

questions.text: Name two mesenchymal tumors of the uterus.
questions.explanation: Leiomyoma is a benign smooth-muscle tumor. Leiomyosarcoma is malignant and generally arises de novo.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma. Endometrial stromal sarcoma is another acceptable example.

questions.text: Enumerate the visceral branches usually described for the internal iliac artery.
questions.explanation: The listed branches supply pelvic viscera and are usually assigned to the anterior division. Branching variants occur.
questions.modelAnswer: The standard visceral branches include the umbilical artery with its superior vesical branches, the middle rectal artery, the inferior vesical artery in males, and the uterine and vaginal arteries in females. The origin of individual branches, particularly the vaginal and middle rectal arteries, can vary.

questions.text: Describe the microscopic features of fibrocystic changes of the breast.
questions.explanation: Cyst formation, fibrosis and adenosis can occur in varying combinations. Epithelial atypia is assessed separately.
questions.modelAnswer: Typical findings include dilated ducts or lobular cysts, often lined by flattened or apocrine epithelium, and variable stromal fibrosis. Adenosis is an increase in acini per lobule. Epithelial hyperplasia may also be present in proliferative patterns.

questions.text: Why is HER2 status evaluated in invasive breast carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Predictive value refers to response to a particular treatment. Prognostic value concerns the expected course of the disease.
questions.modelAnswer: HER2 overexpression or gene amplification identifies a tumor with an activated HER2 pathway. Its main clinical value is predicting eligibility for and likelihood of benefit from HER2-directed treatment. Historically, HER2 positivity was associated with more aggressive disease without effective targeted therapy.

questions.text: Compare the epithelia of the endocervix and ectocervix and explain why cervical precancer commonly arises in the transformation zone.
questions.explanation: The transformation zone is a region of active epithelial remodeling and is the principal area assessed during cervical screening.
questions.modelAnswer: The endocervix has mucus-secreting simple columnar epithelium. The ectocervix is lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium. In the transformation zone, exposed columnar epithelium is replaced by metaplastic squamous epithelium. The immature metaplastic epithelium is a common site for lesions associated with persistent high-risk HPV infection.

questions.text: A urethral smear from a man with purulent urethral discharge shows Gram-negative diplococci within neutrophils. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Intracellular Gram-negative diplococci in a urethral smear from a symptomatic man are characteristic of gonococcal urethritis. Other causes of urethritis do not have this Gram-stain appearance.

questions.text: An adult has bilaterally enlarged kidneys with numerous cysts and affected relatives in successive generations. Which protein is encoded by the gene most often affected in this condition?
questions.explanation: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease most often results from pathogenic variants in PKD1, which encodes polycystin-1. Pathogenic PKD2 variants cause another form.

questions.text: The internal os of the uterus marks the junction between:
questions.explanation: The internal os is the upper opening of the cervical canal into the uterine cavity. The external os opens into the vagina.
options: Uterine tube and fundus of the uterus
Body and Cervix of the uterus
Fundus and body of the uterus

questions.text: A newborn develops mucopurulent conjunctivitis in the second week after birth. Conjunctival epithelial cells show intracytoplasmic inclusions. Which organism best fits?
questions.explanation: Perinatal chlamydial infection can cause conjunctivitis after the first few days of life. Intracytoplasmic inclusions support chlamydial rather than gonococcal or herpetic infection.

questions.text: The duct of the seminal vesicle joins the ductus deferens to form which structure?
questions.explanation: Each ejaculatory duct forms from the duct of a seminal vesicle and the terminal ductus deferens. It passes through the prostate and opens into the prostatic urethra.

questions.text: A postmenopausal patient has vaginal bleeding, endometrial hyperplasia and an ovarian mass. The tumor has microfollicles with Call–Exner bodies. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.explanation: Adult granulosa cell tumors can produce estrogen, causing endometrial proliferation. Microfollicles with Call–Exner bodies support the diagnosis.

questions.text: List four contents of the broad ligament of the uterus.
questions.explanation: The uterine tube occupies the superior free margin. The ovarian attachment and vessels are associated with specific subdivisions of the broad ligament.
questions.modelAnswer: Four examples are the uterine tube, the round ligament of the uterus, the proper ovarian ligament and the uterine vessels. Also acceptable are ovarian vessels running in the relevant folds, the uterovaginal or ovarian nerve plexus, lymphatic vessels and the named mesonephric remnants.

questions.text: Enumerate four constituents of the spermatic cord.
questions.explanation: The ilioinguinal nerve travels alongside the cord through part of the inguinal canal.
questions.modelAnswer: Four examples are the ductus deferens, testicular artery, cremasteric artery and artery to the ductus deferens. The pampiniform plexus, genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, sympathetic fibers and testicular lymphatic vessels are also acceptable.

questions.text: Give two ways in which the prostate contributes to semen or its function after ejaculation.
questions.explanation: Liquefaction helps release sperm from the seminal coagulum. The seminal vesicles contribute a larger share of seminal fluid.
questions.modelAnswer: The prostate contributes a milky, citrate-containing fluid to semen. It also supplies proteases, including prostate-specific antigen, that help liquefy the seminal coagulum after ejaculation.

questions.text: Which vessels and nerve does the ductus deferens cross as it travels along the lateral pelvic wall?
questions.explanation: The ductus deferens also crosses the ureter, but this occurs separately near the base of the bladder.
questions.modelAnswer: It crosses the external iliac artery and vein, the obliterated umbilical artery, the obturator nerve and vessels, and the inferior vesical vessels.

questions.text: Which anatomical segment of the male urethra is the widest?
questions.explanation: The prostatic urethra is the widest and most dilatable segment. It traverses the prostate before continuing into the membranous urethra.

questions.text: Which lymph nodes first receive most lymphatic drainage from the labia majora?
questions.explanation: Lymph from the labia majora drains chiefly to the superficial inguinal nodes. The primary drainage differs from that of the ovaries, which follows the ovarian vessels toward para-aortic nodes.

questions.text: In addition to branches from the inferior vesical artery, which artery commonly contributes to the blood supply of a seminal vesicle?
questions.explanation: The course describes branches from the inferior vesical and middle rectal arteries supplying the seminal vesicle. The other options do not represent its typical direct arterial supply.

questions.text: Which activity of resident vaginal lactobacilli helps maintain a low vaginal pH?
questions.explanation: Lactobacilli ferment glycogen-derived carbohydrates to produce lactic acid. This helps maintain an acidic vaginal environment that contributes to colonization resistance.
options: Release of bicarbonate into the lumen
Degradation of mucus to alkaline amines

questions.text: Which breast lesion features dilated subareolar ducts with inspissated secretions and a plasma-cell-rich periductal infiltrate?
questions.explanation: Duct ectasia involves dilation of the major ducts, retained secretions and chronic periductal inflammation. An intraductal papilloma instead has a papillary proliferation with fibrovascular cores.

questions.text: What is the main developmental effect of fetal anti-Müllerian hormone in a typical male reproductive tract?
questions.explanation: Fetal Sertoli cells produce anti-Müllerian hormone, which causes paramesonephric duct regression. Testosterone promotes mesonephric duct differentiation. DHT is important for masculinization of the external genitalia.

questions.text: A small benign cervical cyst contains retained mucus behind an obstructed endocervical gland opening. What is this lesion called?
questions.explanation: A Nabothian cyst is a mucus-retention cyst. Squamous metaplasia can cover the opening of an endocervical gland so mucus accumulates.

questions.text: A 2-year-old boy has a testicular tumor containing Schiller–Duval bodies. Which serum marker is characteristically elevated in this tumor?
questions.explanation: Schiller–Duval bodies point to a yolk sac tumor, which commonly raises serum alpha-fetoprotein. Human chorionic gonadotropin is characteristic of choriocarcinoma.

questions.text: A 32 year old male presents with very painful genital ulcer and adenopathy. A swab was taken to the lab for tissue culture and revealed multi-nucleated giant cells and intra-nuclear inclusion bodies. What is the causative pathogen?
questions.explanation: Painful genital ulceration with multinucleated giant cells and intranuclear inclusions supports herpes simplex virus infection. The listed bacterial pathogens and HPV do not produce this typical combination.

questions.text: Which embryonic structure gives rise to the seminal vesicle as a diverticulum?
questions.explanation: The seminal vesicle buds from the distal mesonephric, or Wolffian, duct. The segment downstream of this outgrowth contributes to the ejaculatory duct.

questions.text: One paramesonephric duct fails to develop. Which uterine anomaly can result?
questions.explanation: With one paramesonephric duct absent, the other can form a single uterine horn. This results in a unicornuate uterus.

questions.text: Which protein secreted by Sertoli cells helps maintain a high testosterone concentration in the seminiferous tubule?
questions.explanation: Sertoli cells secrete androgen-binding protein into the tubular environment. It binds testosterone and helps maintain the high local concentration needed for spermatogenesis.

questions.text: Which estrogen is the predominant one produced by the placenta during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: The placenta uses steroid precursors supplied by the fetus to produce estriol. Estriol production rises markedly during pregnancy.

questions.text: Which organ lies behind the posterior surface of the prostate, separated from it by rectovesical fascia?
questions.explanation: The posterior surface of the prostate faces the rectum across the rectovesical fascia. This relationship allows the posterior prostate to be felt during a digital rectal examination.

questions.text: Which structure passes close to the upper end of the lateral vaginal fornix, beneath the uterine artery?
questions.explanation: The pelvic ureter passes close to the lateral vaginal fornix. The uterine artery crosses above it lateral to the cervix before supplying the uterus.
